IR 101.description: International Relations.  Basic concepts of world affairs for non-majors. Development ofcompetency to understand and critically evaluate global relationsand international events, stressing empirical approaches. Not available for major credit.

IR 210.description: International Relations: Introductory Analysis. Comprehensive introduction to contending theoretical and analytical approaches; development of critical, evaluative, cognitive, and analytical competencies regarding historical and contemporary issues.

IR 211.description: International Relations: Approaches to Research. Introduction to theoretically oriented research approaches and designs; emphasis on the logic of argumentation.

IR 212.description: Historical Approaches to International Relations. Introduction to historical research methods with an emphasis on historical texts and modes of discourse.

IR 213.description: The Global Economy. Economic and political concepts necessary to the understanding of the modern global economy. Topics include international trade, foreign investment and migration.

IR 304.description: National Intelligence and the Shaping of Policy. The focus is intelligence to improve the making of policy, with attention to collection; overt and covert, operations; domestic intelligence; and oversight in democracies.

IR 305.description: Managing New Global Challenges. Examines the strategies for managing global issues in the post Cold War period. Explores ways that international institutions, national governments and non-state actors work separately and together to provide order and control over complex international issues areas. Issues that will receive attention could include financial and monetary relations, trade and foreign investment, preservation of the environment, the spread of weapons of mass destruction, population and migration, terrori

IR 317.description: The Political Economy of Africa. Understand contemporary outcomes across the African continent; examine the effects of, among others, ecology, the slave trades, European colonialism and geopolitics.

IR 318.description: Violent Conflict . Origins and evolution of violent conflict among humans; modern efforts to end conflict; recent research in archaeology, anthropology, biology, economics, political science and psychology.

IR 319.description: Human Security and Humanitarian Intervention. Explore causes of human security, international  responses to issues like violence, displacement and climate change; and the costs, benefits and effects of humanitarian intervention.

IR 320.description: Technology and International Relations. Impact of technological advances to global security and development. Focus on surveillance and cyber conflict; nuclear weaponry, aviation and UAVs missiles and BMD; submarines and ASW.

IR 330.description: Politics of the World Economy. Exploration of questions and concepts in international economics and politics, especially as they relate to flows of trade, capital, people, and problems across borders.

IR 331.description: The Global Economy 2040. Examination of key ideas from economics, demography and technology. Guest lecturers illuminate possible conditions of the Global Economy in 2040.

IR 332.description: Money, Guns and Oil. Introduction to the relationship between economics, security, and U.S. foreign policy. Topics covered: U.S. grand strategy, Chinas rise, energy security, resource competition, and the resource curse.

IR 339.description: Public Health and International Relations . Examination of threats to global security, state sovereignty and population health posed by infectious diseases, natural disasters, war and civil conflict.

IR 342.description: The Politics and Strategy of Weapons of Mass Destruction. Causes and effects of use and spread of nuclear, biological and chemical weapons; responses to WMD, including deterrence, preventive war, and non-proliferation policies and negotiations.

IR 347.description: Human Rights in Post-Soviet Eurasia. Course examines the struggle for the protection and expansion of human rights in the Post-Communist space across Russia, Ukraine, Caucasus and Central Asia.

IR 357.description: Urban Politics in the Global South. Examination of social and economic justice in the questions of urban governance facing cities in the developing world.

IR 384.description: Asian Security Issues. Introduction to key security trends in the Asia-Pacific region, emphasizing strategic competition between U.S., Russia, and China; regional military capabilities; rise of neutrality politics.

IR 391.description: Directed International Relations Field Study. Intensive internship experience in international relations professional areas with academic research component (may be repeated for credit different semesters)

IR 412.description: Applied Data Science for International Relations 1. Introduction to statistical computing and data visualization in R. Focus on visualization of descriptive statistics; create publication-ready figures for actual faculty research projects.

IR 431.description: Commercial and Financial Globalization-Trends,   Challenges                                      . Factors determining the feasibility, desirability and limits of economic globalization; the dynamics triggered by the Global Financial Crisis and the backlash against Globalization.

IR 436.description: Historical Memory, Identity, and International Politics. Seminar on the role of historical memory in conflicts, in foreign policy formation, and in the creation, alteration, and defense of state identity.

IR 437.description: Comparative Genocide. An interdisciplinary treatment of the tragic phenomenon of genocide. Subject matter includes historical cases and analysis of contemporary global efforts toward prevention.

IR 455.description: The Political Economy of Autocracy. Survey of autocracy, the world's most common form of government: its political economy, the role of elections, parties, repression, propaganda and civil resistance.

IR 457.description: Political Economy of Redistribution. Course examines inequality in the Global South and compares tax and welfare regimes to understand how states pursue redistribution and development.

IR 462.description: State-Building, Institutions in Middle East and North Africa. The interaction of institutions, preferences and historical legacies in the building of state-institutions in the Middle East and North Africa.

IR 490.description: Directed Research.  Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit.

IR 494.description: Honors Thesis Seminar. Preparation and oral defense of senior honors thesis before supervising faculty and fellow honors students. Senior status and acceptance to program required. Recommended preparation: IR 311.

ITAL 012.description: Italian 120 Language Practicum. English grammar as it relates to Italian in order to improve students' Italian language skills; explicit pronunciation and intonation practice. Requires concurrent enrollment in either ITAL 120 Italian I or MPVA 260 Italian Language and Diction.

ITAL 015.description: Italian 150 Language Practicum. English grammar as it relates to Italian in order to improve students Italian language skills; explicit pronunciation and intonation practice.

ITAL 020.description: Course in Reading Italian. For graduate students who wish help in meeting the Italian reading  requirement for the Ph.D. degree. Synoptic presentation of Italian  grammar. Emphasis on development of reading skills. Graded CR/NC.  Not available for degree credit.

ITAL 120.description: Italian I.  Introduction to current Italian. Oral practice, hearing and reading comprehension; grammar necessary for simple spoken and written expression. Lecture, classroom drill, laboratory drill.

ITAL 121.description: Italian Language and Diction. Developing competence in listening, vocal pronunciation, speaking, singing, International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA), reading and writing Italian. Emphasizes musical texts including Italian song and operatic arias.

ITAL 150.description: Italian II. Continuation of Italian I.

ITAL 175.description: Accelerated Italian for Speakers of Spanish and  Other Romance Languages                         . Accelerated introduction to written and spoken Italian for students with a high level of proficiency in Spanish or another Romance Language.  Students completing this course may enroll in the third semester of the basic language sequence ITAL 220.

ITAL 220.description: Italian III. Continuation of Italian II. Review of structure of the language, drill in aural and reading comprehension, practice in oral expression.

ITAL 222.description: Italian Professional Internship: Communication and Culture. Combined classroom discussion and supervised internship at companies. Practical experience in applying communication and cultural knowledge in a professional employment context.

ITAL 240.description: Italian IV. Continuation of Italian III.  Review and expand upon abilities to create with the language in concrete exchanges, descriptions, comparisons, questions and discussions relevant to current issues and topics.

ITAL 300.description: Inventing Modern Italy. An interdisciplinary introduction to the literary, artistic, and  political movements which contributed to the shaping of modern  Italy. Taught in English.

ITAL 490.description: Directed Research.  Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit.

MUJZ 141A.description: Basic Keyboard Skills for the Improviser. Reading skills related to jazz accompanying, including the ability  to identify and play chords on the piano utilizing different  voicings.

MUJZ 150.description: Beginning Jazz Improvisation. Development of beginning improvisational skills including underlying principles of theory, harmony, jazz ear training, and jazz style.

MUJZ 153.description: Individual Instruction. Weekly individual instructio and performance forum.  Open only to  jazz studies majors.

MUJZ 195.description: Jazz Elements I. Study of compositional, improvisational, performance, and  arranging elements found in jazz.  Students will model influential  groups and jazz artists.

MUJZ 197A.description: Vocal Jazz Elements I. Study of stylistic, musical, improvisational, rhythmic, historical, performance, and arranging elements found in the vocal jazz genre. Students will explore concepts through the study of influential jazz vocal artists as well as their own performances.

MUJZ 218A.description: Afro-Latin Percussion Instruments. Instruction in the performance of percussion instruments associated with African, South American, and Caribbean music traditions, with special emphasis on adaptation to jazz music.

MUJZ 218B.description: Afro-Latin Percussion Instruments. Instruction in the performance of percussion instruments associated with African, South American, and Caribbean music traditions, with special emphasis on adaptation to jazz music.

MUJZ 253.description: Individual Instruction. Weekly individual instruction and performance forum.  Open only to  jazz studies majors.

MUJZ 300.description: Non-Major Individual Instruction. Intermediate and advanced instruction designed for non-music  majors.  Not available for credit to music majors.

MUJZ 301.description: Individual Instruction. Intermediate and advanced instruction on secondary instrument for  music majors, on principal instrument for music minors and B.S.  music majors.  Open only to music majors and minors.

MUJZ 305A.description: Advanced Jazz Theory. Analysis and transcription of jazz performances and scores, encompassing questions of style, form, harmonic and melodic language, and considerations of rhythm. Prerequisites: MUCO 133b.

MUJZ 353.description: Individual Instruction. Weekly individual instruction and performance forum.  Open only to  jazz studies majors.

MUJZ 395.description: Jazz Elements II. Advanced study of compositional, improvisational, performance, conducting, and arranging elements found in the jazz repertory. Students will be encouraged to forge individual musical expressions.

MUJZ 400.description: Arranging for Jazz Ensemble.  Scoring for jazz ensemble with emphasis on writing for sections of like and mixed instruments as well as full ensemble.

MUJZ 443.description: Jazz Pedagogy.  Concepts, methods, and resources; examination and comparison of textbooks, recordings, tapes, and materials related to the study and teaching of jazz.

MUJZ 450.description: Intermediate Jazz Improvisation. Development of intermediate improvisational skills including underlying principles of theory, harmony, jazz ear training, and jazz style. Recommended preparation: MUJZ 150.

MUJZ 453.description: Individual Instruction. Weekly individual instruction and performance forum.  Open only to  jazz studies majors.

MUJZ 490.description: Directed Research.  Individual research and readings. No available for graduate credit.

MUJZ 501.description: Individual Instruction. Secondary instruction for graduate music majors or instruction for  graduate non-music majors.

MUJZ 547.description: Jazz Composition.  Application of theoretical and compositional techniques used in jazz to written music. Analysis and performance of historical and contemporary examples will be included.

MUJZ 554.description: Graduate Certificate Performance. Individual instruction and related lab participation for Graduate  Certificate students.

MUJZ 590.description: Directed Research.  Research leading to the Master's Degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

MUJZ 653.description: Performance.  Individual or master class instruction for D.M.A. Performance majors.

MUJZ 790.description: Research. Research leading to the doctorate.  Maximum units which may be  applied to the degree to be determined by the department.  Graded  CR/NC.

JOUR 200.description: The Power and Responsibility of the Press. Explores the role of journalism and social media in society - its influence on government, technology, business, national security, sports, science and entertainment.

JOUR 201.description: Culture of Journalism: Past, Present and Future. Examines the social, cultural and political aspects of U.S. journalism over time and currently.

JOUR 205.description: Journalism Practicum. Field experience in journalism, public relations, or related field.

JOUR 206.description: Reporting and Writing Practicum. Experiential lab in which students report, write and produce digital journalism content and report and produce live radio/television broadcasts in a student-led newsroom.

JOUR 207.description: Reporting and Writing I. Journalism fundamentals, including news judgment,  finding and verifying information, and reporting and writing.

JOUR 210.description: Basics of News Production for Non-Majors. Introduction to television, radio, and/or digital news production. Examination of issues in journalism.

JOUR 300.description: Journalism and Society. Examination of media and society by applying concepts on power, ideology, discourse and representation to specific case studies from the field and practice of journalism.

JOUR 307.description: Reporting and Writing II. Report, write, produce and distribute in-depth stories, including longer news and analysis pieces.

JOUR 320.description: Introduction to Coding for Storytelling. Introduction to basic web technologies; conceive, design, code and produce an advanced multimedia story package.

JOUR 321.description: Visual Journalism. Basics of visual journalism, including video storytelling and photography.

JOUR 322.description: Introduction to Investigative and Data Journalism. Reportorial and analytical skills and techniques required for portraying and evaluating contemporary newsworthy events using basic data journalism techniques and tools for statistical analysis.

JOUR 330.description: Photojournalism. Emphasis on fundamental skills necessary for photojournalism  including camera techniques, story ideas and digital darkroom.

JOUR 350.description: Introduction to Sports Media. Highlight norms, routines of content, including print, broadcast, video. Focus on opportunities, constraints posed by roles of reporters, fans, players, publicists, agents, leagues, teams.

JOUR 372.description: Engaging Diverse Communities. Covers strategies of community engagement and beat reporting.

JOUR 381.description: Entertainment, Business and Media in Today's Society. An examination of the symbiotic relationship of the entertainment  business and the media; press coverage of the entertainment  industry; Hollywood's relationship with news media.

JOUR 402.description: Advanced Video Reporting. Role of the broadcast journalism reporter; similarities and differences between print and electronic media; application of audio-video equipment; analysis and practical experience.

JOUR 403.description: Television News and Sports Production. Production of television news and sports programs while developing video, writing and communication skills and managing content in collaboration with others under deadline pressure.

JOUR 404.description: Produce and Host Sports Content in Studio A. Interview, present and design sports segments for television/video in Studio A.

JOUR 405.description: Non-Fiction Television. Presentation and selection in non-fiction television programs including documentaries, electronic magazines and news series; ethical problems, field research, reporting, interviewing, pre-production.

JOUR 407.description: The World of Podcasting. Concentrates on practical, hands-on skills for the production and distribution of a non-fiction podcast.

JOUR 414.description: Advanced Digital Media Storytelling. An advanced single-topic multimedia package.

JOUR 425.description: Advanced Radio News Production. Production of public radio news: producing real-time newscasts for Annenberg Radio News. Newsgathering, assigning stories, anchoring, interviewing, working with reporters, editing and producing live programming.

JOUR 431.description: Feature Writing. Techniques of writing newspaper feature stories, including the profile, the light feature, the news feature, the in-depth story; the art of narrative writing.

JOUR 432.description: Sports Commentary. Techniques of reporting and writing sports columns and commentary for print, video, radio and Web-based media.

JOUR 441.description: Sports Reporting. News and feature coverage of sporting events, including social and economic factors influencing sports in America.

JOUR 446.description: Entertainment Reporting. Techniques of reporting and writing about the entertainment business, economics and finances. Analysis of the skills and background needed for reporters specializing in this area of the news.

JOUR 448.description: Government and Public Affairs Reporting. Techniques for covering beats that are the foundation of daily newspaper reporting, including crime, education, immigration and local government.

JOUR 458.description: Media, Food and Culture. Analyzes the ways media tell the story of our food and examines the critical issues surrounding what we eat.

JOUR 462.description: Law of Mass Communication. Covers the First Amendment and case law establishing journalists' freedoms and providing the framework for the practice of the craft.

JOUR 469.description: Money, Markets and Media. Practical approach to understanding and writing about economic concepts through current events, case studies and historical examples.

JOUR 479.description: Storytelling for Action Sports. Learn how to cover action sports with cutting-edge technology. In-class lectures and industry guest speakers focus on topics such as gender, race and history.

JOUR 481.description: The Athlete, Sports Media and Popular Culture. Analysis of the images of the athlete and sports media helps us understand how sports dramatically affects such social issues as race, class and gender.

JOUR 486.description: Multiplatform Olympic and Paralympic Storytelling. Develop the skills necessary to produce multiplatform coverage of mega-events like the Olympic and Paralympic Games.

JOUR 487.description: Power, Players & Platforms in Global Sports. Go inside the leagues, teams, companies, and streaming platforms to understand how sports are sold, broadcast, and integrated into the fabric of our lives.

JOUR 490.description: Directed Research.  Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit.

JOUR 491.description: News Leadership. Brutal economics, labor-management tensions, DEI, lawsuit threats -- learn how news leaders juggle all this and more while inspiring their staff to produce great journalism.

JOUR 499.description: Special Topics.  Selected topics in journalism.

JOUR 510.description: Special Assignment Reporting. Beat reporting with a deep dive into research, source development, and writing/reporting skills. Focus on current trends, history, major actors and key issues.

JOUR 521.description: Documentary Pre-Production. Pre-production of video documentary including selection of topic, diversity, ethical and legal problems, research and reporting techniques, interviewing, writing, balanced presentation, visual and audio literacy.

JOUR 531.description: Fall Digital Journalism Immersion. Students write, report, produce, code, promote (through social media) and publish/air cross-platform stories in a converged news environment.

JOUR 532.description: Fall Digital Journalism Immersion Practicum. Report, write and distribute in-depth stories for diverse audiences; enhance understanding of news judgment; develop and maintain sources; engage communities through field reporting.

JOUR 539.description: Introduction to Investigative Reporting. Focus on basic investigative reporting; understand its history, how to access records, identify sources, use computer assisted reporting, report in a fair and ethical manner.

JOUR 552.description: Video Reporting and Production. Writing, reporting and producing content for video and digital platforms; similarities and differences between media; application of audio-visual and digital equipment.

JOUR 553.description: Coding and Programming for Storytelling. Sketch, design and code a website from scratch, using HTML, CSS and jQuery plug-ins to tell a rich multimedia story. Open only to journalism majors.

JOUR 556.description: Digital Investigations I: Introduction to OSINT Reporting. Introduction to open-source investigations, including how to leverage publicly available sources of online information to uncover stories, verify claims and investigate complex issues.

JOUR 567.description: The Power of Narrative. Explores outstanding narrative journalism across wide range of platforms, subjects. Through readings, discussions, guest lecture "salons," students learn reporting, writing skills necessary for in-depth storytelling.

JOUR 579.description: Journalism Internship. Field experience in journalism, public relations, or related field.

JOUR 587.description: Los Angeles Culture: 1960 to Today. Explore how Los Angeles culture evolved from Eurocentrism to a distinct Multiculturalism that reflects one of the most diverse cities in the world.

JOUR 590.description: Directed Research.  Research leading to the Master's degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

JOUR 592.description: Arts Journalism: Storytelling and Production. Reporting and writing on the arts; strategies for arts journalism in the digital era; survey of essays and reviews by great critics.

JOUR 594A.description: Master's Thesis.  Credit on acceptance of thesis.

JOUR 594Z.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of thesis. Graded IP/CR/NC.

JOUR 595.description: Critical Thinking: The Art and Science of Not Getting Fooled. Researching and writing about how not to get fooled as a journalist; includes research, writing and discussion. Open only to journalism and specialized journalism majors.

JOUR 599.description: Special Topics. Seminar in selected topics in journalism.

JS 100.description: Jewish History. Major ideas, personalities, and movements in Jewish history from antiquity to the present in light of the interaction of the Jews with the general culture.

JS 180.description: Judaism. Jewish beliefs, practices, and history from the biblical period to the present; Judaic contributions to Western civilization.

JS 211.description: The Holocaust.  Historical background and responses to the Holocaust, withspecial emphasis on ethical implications.

JS 258.description: Food and Faith. Investigates how food and food traditions create and traverse religious and social relationships between Jews, Christians and Muslims by exploring religious traditions, practice, and ethics.

JS 310.description: The Eastern European Jewish Experience: Literature and Film. Analyzes works by different artists -- writers, filmmakers, painters -- in order to understand the significant contribution that the Jewish experience in Eastern Europe has made to Jewish communities worldwide.

JS 314.description: Holy War And History: Jews, Christians, Muslims. Investigates the engagement in war by Judaism, Christianity and Islam by examining history and theology and looks at religious justifications and condemnations of war.

JS 345.description: Representing: Contemporary Sephardic and Mizrahi Jews. Jewish experience outside of Europe is explored through film and literature. Topics include Jewish-Muslim relations, Orientalism, transnationalism, linguistic histories, notions of homeland and gender.

JS 361.description: Scripture and Polemic in Judaism, Christianity and Islam. Origins of Scriptures and their polemical environments in earliest Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. Scripture as polemic and legitimation, and cross-religious/cross-cultural interpretation and argument based on scriptural themes.

JS 379.description: Mixing and Matching: Intermarriage in 21st Century. An investigation into inter-ethnic, interracial, and inter-religious marriage in the 21st century.

JS 490.description: Directed Research.  Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit.

JS 590.description: Directed Research.  Research leading to the master's degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

LAT 120.description: Latin I. Essentials of Latin grammar and vocabulary.

LAT 150.description: Latin II. Essentials of Latin grammar and vocabulary, continued.  Basic  reading skills.

LAT 222.description: Latin III. Reading Latin literature.  Introduction to reading and translation  of classical Latin prose and poetry.  Extensive grammar review.

LAT 490.description: Directed Research.  Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit. Prerequisite: consent of instructor.

LAW 150.description: Stereotypes, Prejudice and the Rule of Law. Examines how stereotypes and prejudice undermine equal justice under the law but also how creative word work and art can promote racial justice.

LAW 200.description: Law and Society. Sources and structure of law; history of Bill of Rights emphasizing effect on criminal justice system; limits of law in solving problems in American society.

LAW 201.description: Law and Politics. Examination of the rules and realities of American politics, and the role politics plays in American life and culture.

LAW 205.description: Introduction to Criminal Law. Provides a comprehensive analysis of the criminal justice system and an overview of the fundamentals of substantive criminal law.

LAW 206.description: Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence: Ethics and Law. Analyzes the ethical dilemmas and societal implications of artificial intelligence and debates the future of artificial intelligence regulations and laws.

LAW 207.description: Personal Data in the 21st Century. Examine how governments and corporations confront information privacy conflicts. Analyze various perspectives on information privacy laws and their place in society.

LAW 210.description: Fundamentals of the U.S. Legal System. Introduces the U.S. legal system and its relationship to basic principles of the rule of law. Examines lawmaking institutions, judicial processes and contemporary legal issues.

LAW 212.description: Immigration Law for a New America. Examines current immigration law in America, the normative debates over immigration policies and the role the government plays in expanding or limiting immigration rights.

LAW 220.description: The Legal Profession. Introduces students to the basic aspects of the legal profession.

LAW 222.description: Interdisciplinary Perspectives on the Law. Examines law and the legal system from different disciplinary perspectives. It explores how various disciplines provide different insights to the legal regime.

LAW 300.description: Concepts in American Law. The main concepts and topics in American law, in the historical, economic and cultural contexts in which they have developed.

LAW 305.description: International Influence: Law and Power. Examination of the philosophic and political concepts that underpin international influence, while learning how this structure impacts the modern incentives and interests of international actors.

LAW 306.description: Issues in the Use of AI in Law and Regulation. Focuses on the role artificial intelligence plays in a variety of aspects of the law through humanities-based approaches like ethics, linguistics, sociological and economics approaches.

LAW 307.description: Love, Sex, Money, and Power: How Law Shapes Families. Examines how the law affects lovers, spouses, parents, and children from multiple perspectives, including racial justice, feminism, morality, economics, and legal theory.

LAW 324.description: Sports Law. Examines the relevance and application of legal structures to all participants in the sports enterprise by providing an overview of legal and ethical issues.

LAW 352.description: Introduction to Law and Economics. An exploration of core aspects of the US legal system (property, contracts, torts, criminal law, civil procedure) from the perspective of basic economics theory.

LAW 401.description: Cybersecurity and Cybercrime. Studies the rise of cybercrimes and cybersecurity measures in recent years and their impact on society. Topics include cyberattacks, digital forensics, information privacy and others.

LAW 402.description: Psychology and Law. Explores issues of responsibility and credibility.  Intentional  and unintentional behavior.  Clinical biases.  Topics include  witness credibility, confessions, cults, hostages, battered  persons, and repressed memories.

LAW 490.description: Directed Research. Individual research and readings.

LAW 492.description: Undergraduate Law Review. Introduces students to the basics of legal writing and research, with a focus on legal scholarship and law review-type journal articles.

LAW 497.description: Legal Studies Capstone Project. A cumulative experience demonstrating a student's depth of knowledge in applying research and writing skills on examining the legal system.

LAW 498.description: Law Internship. Intensive law-related experience with a non-profit organization, public agency, government agency or private company.

LAW 500O.description: Overseas Studies. Off campus coursework; title of course taken at host institution  appears as a section title.

LAW 502.description: Procedure I. Consideration of the participants in litigation; private and public plaintiffs, defendants, and courts. Information exchange, process, outcomes, and costs of lawsuits.

LAW 503.description: Contracts. The interpretation and enforcement of promises and agreements.

LAW 504.description: Criminal Law.  The crime problem and the legislative response to it through substantive criminal law; administration of criminal justice through police, prosecutorial, sentencing, and penological discretion.

LAW 505.description: Legal Profession. Functions of the lawyer in modern society; history and organization of the legal profession; the adversary system; equal access to justice; other problems of ethics and professional responsibility.

LAW 508.description: Constitutional Law: Structure. Considers the delineation of spheres of responsibility between the judiciary and legislature, the nation and the state, and the government and the individual.

LAW 509.description: Torts I. Individual's obligation not to harm others; bases for compensating persons who are harmed, either by holding responsible whoever is at fault or by invoking other principles of liability, including the efficiency of resource allocation and the spreading of losses.

LAW 510.description: Legal Research. Examination of the basic sources of law for federal and California jurisdictions, utilizing a vast array of sources from books to     computer-assisted research and analyzing research methodology and  techniques. Graded CR/D/F.

LAW 511A.description: Legal Writing. Two-semester course focusing on developing analytic and communication skills. Lawyers will analyze legal principles and incisively apply them to facts. Graded CR/D/F.

LAW 513.description: Effective Writing for Professionals. Focuses on professional writing structure based on audience, tone, form and purpose.

LAW 515.description: Legal Research, Writing, and Advocacy I. Development of legal research, writing, and advocacy skills.   Emphasis on objective legal writing, including memoranda, and  researching case law through primary and secondary sources.   Registration restricted to Law students.

LAW 520.description: Introduction to U.S. Legal System. The basic structure of government in the U.S., including the  constitutionally mandated division of power in the federal  government and the federal system of power sharing between state  and federal systems.  A comparative perspective on selected  substantive and procedural matters, such as common law reasoning,  jury trials, adversary process, and various aspects of civil  procedure.  Open to incoming LL.M. students only.

LAW 521.description: Topics in American Law. This course will provide LL.M. and M.C.L. students with a survey  of various topics in American law including criminal law,  evidence, family law, constitutional law, torts, wills and trusts,  administrative law and property law.  Open to LL.M. and M.C.L.  students only.

LAW 522.description: Entertainment Law and Industry. Provides a detailed survey of entertainment law, entertainment-related transactions and litigation, and legal issues facing the entertainment industry.

LAW 530.description: Fundamental Business Principles. Exposes students to everyday business and finance vocabulary, concepts and modes of analysis. Strongly recommended for students without significant prior business experience. Graded CR/D/F.

LAW 532.description: Constitutional Law: Rights. Examines constitutional rights particularly ones protected under the Equal Protection/Due Process Clauses and related questions of judicial role and theories of interpretation.

LAW 550.description: Law for Business. A student-run periodical that publishes student-written and peer-edited  articles relevant to the intersection between law and business.

LAW 552.description: Law and the Fundamentals of AI. Provides a robust understanding of artificial intelligence, emphasizing its relevance and applications in the legal domain and delves into the foundational concepts of AI.

LAW 554.description: AI Ethics, Privacy and Regulation. Explores the ethical, legal and privacy implications involved with using Artificial Intelligence focused on case law, statutes and current and proposed AI regulations.

LAW 559.description: Human Resource Compliance. Provides an overview of human resource related law, and various legal issues involved in the employment relationship.

LAW 560.description: Academic and Professional Skills for U.S. Law Studies I. Explores and develops the legal communication and analytical skills necessary to the practice of law.

LAW 561A.description: Fundamentals of Legal Writing Skills. Explores purpose and form of legal documents and emphasizes effective communication.

LAW 563.description: Presentation Skills for International Lawyers. Explores the art of public speaking and effective communication in legal settings.

LAW 565.description: U.S. Common Law Analysis and Skills. Explores how judicial opinions interact with other sources of law and develop law in the United States.

LAW 567.description: Introduction to Litigation in U.S. Courts. Provides an overview of the United States legal system for those unfamiliar with common law courts, including the mechanics of the U.S. Court system in both criminal and civil courts, as well as more detailed analysis of torts and intellectual property disputes.

lectures.instructor: Bahaar Cadambi; Jason Morris; Anitha Cadambi
Bahaar Cadambi; Jason Morris; Anitha Cadambi

LAW 579.description: Global Regulatory Compliance. Introduction to regimes that regulate business practices on a global level and compliance of such regimes, such as Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, OECD Anti-Bribery Convention, and other regulations.

LAW 596.description: Internship for Curricular Practical Training. Part-time or full-time, practical work experience in the student's field of study. The internship must be located at an off-campus facility. Students are individually supervised by faculty. May not be taken until the student has completed at least one semester of enrollment in the graduate program with a cumulative 3.0 GPA.

LAW 597.description: Environmental Policy and Natural Resources Law. Introduces environmental policy and natural resources law, surveying treatment of biodiversity, fisheries, water, protected lands, forests, and the general themes and conflicts of environmental management.

LAW 598.description: Regulatory Compliance. Provides an overview of regulatory compliance law and the ways that various organizations ensure compliance with governing laws and regulations.

lectures.instructor: Christopher Mardesich; Anitha Cadambi; Anna Badua

LAW 600.description: Taxation.  Federal tax statutes, technical issues and social problems involved in tax planning, tax litigation, and reform of the tax laws.

LAW 602.description: Criminal Procedure. Criminal procedure in the courts, and the regulation of lawenforcement by the courts through rules of evidence andinterpretation of the Bill of Rights.

LAW 603.description: Business Organizations. Organization of economic activity especially the modern corporation as institutions of social power. The roles of managers, owners, and regulatory agencies in shaping processes ofdecision making.

LAW 605.description: Real Estate Transactions and Finance. An in-depth look at the most prevalent transactions and finance tools related to both residential and commercial real estate. Topics include: purchase and sale of realty; property valuation; brokerage agreements; land conveyance and the recording acts; escrows, title insurance and closings; investment vehicles and deal structures; mortgage lending and commercial finance; and foreclosures.

LAW 607.description: Gifts, Wills, and Trusts.  Gratuitous transfer of wealth, especially the transmission of wealth from one generation to the next as a settlement of family affairs. Comparative analysis of the legal mechanisms of gifts, wills, and trusts. Introduction to problems of fiduciary administration.

LAW 608.description: Evidence. The purpose and character of trial. Problems of adversary presentation and the nature of proof. The basis for admission and exclusion of evidence in judicial proceedings.

LAW 616.description: Practicing Commercial Real Estate Transactional  Law. Provides an in-depth exposure to the practice of commercial real estate transactional law, including an analysis of the differing perspectives of each side of a transaction and a hands-on study of how lawyers negotiate and document various types of commercial real estate transactions.

LAW 619.description: Disability Rights Law and Practical Skills. Examines the various federal and California state laws addressing discrimination on the basis of disability from a litigators perspective, emphasizing both substantive law as well as legal practice skills.

LAW 622.description: Money in Politics. Studies the statutes and cases governing campaign finance in America and the latest research into their effects.

LAW 623.description: Family Law. Creating, regulating and dissolving family relationships. Explore moral and power relations among men, women, children, and the State. Develop skills to help clients in families.

LAW 625.description: Remedies. Comparison of the remedial goals of contracts, torts, and property and the impact of procedural devices in law and equity. Damages, injunctions, specific performance and restitution. Remedial theory and transactional application.

LAW 630.description: Mediation Clinic I. Students receive the training required to become professional mediators for civil cases in the L.A. County Superior Court, and mediate these cases.

LAW 632.description: Business for Lawyers. This course introduces law students to the tools, concept, and language of business. It is premised on the belief that to excel as a business lawyer, one must understand the business world from the perspective of the clients one counsels and assists. The course will cover, in compressed form, the basic subjects from the MBA program which are most useful to lawyers.  Open only to law  students.

LAW 634.description: Legal Analysis of Evidence. Legal analysis of the rules of Evidence using problems designed to improve analytic skills and problem-solving. Taken in conjunction with Evidence.

LAW 635.description: Employment Discrimination Law. Examines the regulation of employment discrimination under federal law. Pays primary attention to issues of race, sex, age and disability discrimination.

LAW 637.description: International Trade Policy. Examination of the institutions and laws that regulate international economic relations. Students will be introduced to the major international agreements and national laws that regulate international trade goods, services and capital.

LAW 638.description: Trauma-Informed Lawyering. An introduction of trauma and trauma-informed practice within the  legal field. Learn the skills to represent trauma survivors and  address vicarious trauma.

LAW 642.description: Secured Transactions. This is a course on Chattel paper and secured transactions involving personal property under Article 9 of the Uniform Commerical Code and some related bodies of law.

LAW 643.description: Social Movement Lawyering Practicum. Disassembling structural racism using law, research and community organizing through work with the Coalition for Property Tax Justice.

LAW 647.description: Bankruptcy: Debtors and Creditors I.  Bankruptcy of the poor, imprudent or unlucky, and of unsuccessful business. The mechanisms of our law for distributing the debtor's property and discharging his obligations.

LAW 648.description: Topics in Entertainment Law. Contemporary topics in the field of entertainment law.

LAW 650.description: Entertainment Law. An examination of how the courts are handling selected, "cutting edge" topics in entertainment law. The topics will include the scope of and limitations on the right of publicity; fair use and parody defenses to copyright infringement; future technology clauses in rights contracts; and copyright and defamation issues arising in the online world. Previous entertainment law courses recommended, but not required.

LAW 652.description: Computer Crime Law. Examines the legal and policy issues involved with the emergence of cyber crimes and cyber security issues, including government access and privacy issues.

LAW 653.description: Music Law in Practice. Focus on contract drafting and negotiation issues relevant to an artist's pursuit of a career in the music business.

LAW 654.description: Television and Digital Media. An in-depth study of television industry legal concepts, contracts, business structures and economic models.

LAW 658.description: Mergers and Acquisitions. Problems of integrating the corporate, securities, tax, business,  antitrust, accounting and contractual aspects of corporate mergers and aquisitions.

LAW 662.description: Public International Law. Principles of international law involving relations among governments. The function of international tribunals and organizations.

LAW 665.description: Art Law. Provides an overview, often from a litigation perspective, of      legal issues affecting artworks and cultural property.

LAW 666A.description: Trademark Moot Court. An intensive, two-semester course preparing students interested in U.S. trademark and unfair competition law for participation in the annual Saul Lefkowitz Moot Court Competition.

LAW 667.description: Hale Moot Court Brief. Invitation-only course offered to second-year students as part of  the Hale Moot Court Honors Program. Students write an appellate  brief.

LAW 669.description: Moot Court Supervision. Evaluation and supervision of the preparation of briefs and oral arguments in the Hale Moot Court honors competition.

LAW 678A.description: Review of Law and Social Justice Staff. Writing, source-checking, and preliminary editing of articles and  comments for publication in the Review of Law and Social Justice.   For second year students serving as staff members on the Review.   Open to law students only.  Graded CR/D/F.

LAW 679.description: Review of Law and Social Justice Writing. Writing, source-checking and preliminary editing of articles and comments for publication in the Review of Law and Social Justice.

LAW 680.description: Mediation Theory and Practice. Develop knowledge and skills associated with the mediation process as a third party neutral. Explore mediation theories, practices, ethical issues and policies.

LAW 680A.description: Review of Law and Social Justice Editing. Supervision of research and writing, and final editing of articles  and comments for publication in the Review of Law and Social  Justice.  For officers of the Review.  Open to law students only.   Graded IP to CR/D/F.

LAW 694.description: Cyberlaw: Legal Issues Impacting Providers and Users of Inte. An overview of common legal issues impacting both providers and users of Internet services.

LAW 695.description: Criminal Law in Social Context (Seminar). Contextualizes criminal law through analyzing the legal and social  characterizations of "victims" and "perpetrators" in U.S. law,  politics and popular culture.

LAW 696.description: Topics in Business Organizations Law. Legal analysis of selected sub-topics of business organizations  law using problems designed to improve analytic skills and  problem-solving. Taken in conjunction with Business Organizations.

LAW 698.description: Equity and the Legal and Social Determinants of Health. Explores how legal, social, racial, cultural and economic factors contribute to health disparities and the role that physicians and lawyers can play in advocating for patients and policy changes to promote health equity.

LAW 699.description: Advanced Trial Advocacy: Trial Competition Team. Provides hands-on training in jury persuasion, case theory, examinations, arguments, evidence, and courtroom advocacy, culminating in national trial competitions.

LAW 701.description: Child Interviewing Practicum. Learn how to effectively interview child witnesses. Students will practice mock interviews, and may be eligible to conduct actual interviews of child witnesses.

LAW 705.description: Community Property. The law of community property, including disposition of property on dissolution of the marriage and questions of conflict of laws.

LAW 708.description: Contract Drafting, Analysis and Negotiation. Covers the fundamentals of reviewing and analyzing business contracts and strategies for negotiating business issues with an emphasis on developing practical skills. Open only to Law students.

LAW 709.description: Contract Drafting and Negotiation. Contract drafting and negotiating will teach students the   mechanics of drafting and negotiating sophisticated contracts from  a variety of legal disciplines including entertainment law, real  estate law and general corporate law.

LAW 710.description: Contract Drafting and Analysis. Students present to the class their assessment of assigned contracts, then draft their own contracts, interpret a complex contract, followed by team-based rewrites.

LAW 712.description: Negotiation Theory and Application. Develops enhanced negotiation skills and a working understanding of ADR processes and procedures in an interactive classroom experience.

LAW 715.description: ADR Law and Policy: Mediation and Arbitration. Exploration of the origin, development, and practice of mediation, arbitration and other forms of ADR, emphasizing the policies       underlying these increasingly significant and evolving areas.

LAW 717.description: Estate Planning. Legal and tax considerations important to the lawyers advising  their clients on the transmission of wealth from one generation to  the next.

LAW 719.description: Corporate Finance. Legal and economic aspects of corporate finance including capital structure, policy, mergers, takeovers, and freeze-outs; analysis of policy relating to present law and possible reforms.

LAW 721.description: Crime, Punishment and Justice. Explores the nature and evolution of criminal punishment, from the death penalty to imprisonment and beyond.

LAW 725.description: American Exceptionalism and Polarization. Explores the interrelationship between American exceptionalism and the growing polarization of American society.

LAW 737.description: Small Business Clinic II. Continuation of Small Business Clinic I.  Open to Law students  only.

LAW 738.description: E-Discovery Law. Focuses on the electronic storage of information (ESI) and how it works in the litigation discovery process.

LAW 740.description: Real Estate Contracts. An overview of commerical real estate transactions with a focus on  drafting, analyzing, negotiating, and revising legal documents  needed to close a deal.

LAW 743.description: Federal Criminal Law. Covered topics include offenses relating to fraud and political corruption, terrorism, narcotics, money laundering, organized crime, false statements and obstruction of justice.

LAW 749.description: Securities Regulation. Regulation by state and federal agencies of issuance of, and trading in, stocks, bonds, and other securities. Particular reference to SEC regulations.

LAW 755.description: Contemporary Name, Image and Likeness. Examines the history and legal foundation of Name, Image, and  Likeness in college athletics, culminating in simulated NIL  contract negotiations.

LAW 759.description: Elder Law and Justice Practicum. Examines the multifactorial issues facing the growing aging  population and the common legal concerns that arise in  representing older adults through coursework and experential  practice.

LAW 760A.description: Interdisciplinary Law Journal Staff. Source-checking and preliminary editing of articles and comments  for publication in the Interdisciplinary Law Journal. For  second-year students serving as staff members on the Journal.  Graded IP/CR/NC.

LAW 761.description: Interdisciplinary Law Journal Writing. Students will write journal notes as members of the Interdisciplinary Law Journal.

LAW 762A.description: Interdisciplinary Law Journal Editing. Supervision and final editing of articles and comments for publication in the Interdisciplinary Law Journal.  Graded IP to  CR/69/65.

LAW 763.description: Federal Courts: The Federal System II. Problems of adjudication in a federal system. Allocation of authority between federal and state courts and among Congress, the Executive and the Courts; choice of federal and state law; jurisdiction of federal courts and significant rules of practice.

LAW 764.description: International Business Transactions.  Survey of legal aspects of international trade and investment transactions, including tax considerations.

LAW 765.description: Intellectual Property Litigation. Analyzes selected contributions to intellectual property scholarship and explores some challenging problems in contemporary intellectual property law.

LAW 766.description: Writing for Publication Seminar. Special seminars to provide a forum for students who wish to produce a paper for academic publication to receive guidance and feedback.

LAW 767A.description: Law Review Staff. Writing, source- checking, and preliminary editing of articles and comments for publication in the Southern California Law Review. For second year students serving as staff members on the Review. Graded IZ..

LAW 768.description: Law Review Writing. Writing, source-checking and preliminary editing of articles and comments for publication in the Southern California Law Review.

LAW 769A.description: Law Review Editing.  Supervision of research and writing, and final editing of articles and comments for publication in the Southern California Law Review. For officers of the Review. Graded IP to CR/69/65.

LAW 772.description: Intellectual Property.  The protection of intellectual property and encouragement of creativity. Explores copyright, trademarks, patents, and selected state law theories.

LAW 775.description: Immigration Law.  Development of immigration law to its present state.

LAW 776.description: Immigration Clinic I. Students represent clients before Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the Immigration Court, and certain law enforcement agencies in cases including applications for relief under the Violence Against Women Act, for asylum, and for relief against deportation. Open only to LAW students.

LAW 777.description: Administrative Law and Regulatory Policy. Legal principles subject to judicial control and the alternative   ways in which agencies can be organized to serve their purposes.

LAW 779.description: Entertainment Disputes. An exploration of litigation and dispute resolution in the  entertainment industry, ranging from traditional conflicits to  emerging issues.

LAW 781.description: Externship I. An externship allows a student to gain hands-on legal experience in legal settings. Students will be assigned to a legal services program, government agency, or state or federal judge under faculty supervision. All externships include a classroom component.

LAW 782.description: Externship II. Advanced externship. All externships include a classroom component.

LAW 784.description: The Law and Economics of the US-China Tech Rivalry. This seminar examines a broad spectrum of legal areas where the  United States and China have clashed in their ongoing rivalry to  claim technological supremacy.

LAW 785.description: Global Regulation of Artificial Intelligence. This course explores the challenges posed by generative artificial  intelligence across various areas of law and evaluates the  regulatory responses from major jurisdictions.

LAW 786.description: Advanced Externships. Advanced externships consist of field work at a placement and a  bi-weekly instructed course. Assignments are designed to support  professional growth as a law student.

LAW 789.description: Race, Racism and the Law. Understand the reciprocal relationship through which race and racism have shaped American law and how law has shaped popular conceptions of race and racism.

LAW 790.description: Artificial Intelligence in Litigation and Dispute Resolution. Explores AIs impact on dispute resolution, emphasizing practical skills in litigation, negotiation, evidence, risk assessment, ethics, and AI-enabled legal strategy.

LAW 793.description: International Taxation. Explores taxation of inbound and outbound international  transactions, including source rules, the Foreign Tax Credit,  Subpart F, taxation of intangible income, and other topics.

LAW 797.description: Law and Social Science Seminar. An introduction to cutting-edge social-science research about law  which meets, in part, in conjunction with Center for Law & Social  Science (CLASS) workshops.

LAW 799.description: The Role of the In-House Entertainment Lawyer. Hands-on experience performing legal work on a hypothetical  television program. The class will act as the legal department  under supervision of the department head (instructor).

LAW 804.description: Information Privacy Law. Surveys the legal framework concerning information privacy in the US, including developments in constitutional, tort, contract, property and statutory law to address emerging privacy threats.

LAW 810.description: Patent Law. Patent laws, litigation, and the process of prosecuting the patent application. The concept of invention and ownership of rights under patents.

LAW 811.description: Health Law and Policy. Explores the statutes and regulations that govern the health care system and the policies that shape its development.

LAW 814.description: Topics in Tort Theory Seminar. Enduring questions in the theory and practice of torts and related  fields. Topics to vary by semester.

LAW 819.description: ADR Ethics. Provides law students, lawyers and professional neutrals with an in-depth examination of the rules guiding our behavior in various dispute resolution processes. Open only to law students.

LAW 820.description: Pretrial Advocacy. Examines conceptual and practical aspects of interviewing,         counseling, negotiation, settlement, drafting and formal advocacy  in the handling of legal cases.

LAW 821.description: Trial Advocacy. Examines decicion-making by counsel in the litigation of cases. Emphasis is given to decisions involving tactics, strategies, and their implications for the functioning of legal institutions and substantive doctrine. Extensive use of simulated trial practice exercises.

LAW 827.description: Counseling the Startup Company. Role of the attorney in startup firms: business plan, employment  agreements, lease, stock option plan, financing documents and  distribution and strategic partnership arrangements.  Enrollment  restricted to law students.

LAW 833.description: Labor Arbitration. Introduces students to the National Labor Relations Act, collective bargaining and the labor arbitration process. Students also prepare labor arbitration briefs. Open only to Law students.

LAW 845.description: Negotiation Skills. Develops students' negotiating skills through role plays, reflection and instructor feedback.

LAW 847.description: Law of Sports Event and Facility Management. Covers legal and business issues of sport facilities and event operations, combining legal and business strategies and practices around contracting, corporate partnerships, and risk management.

LAW 849.description: International Human Rights Clinic I. Students work under close faculty supervision on cases and projects that involve the application of international law to address human rights violations.

LAW 856.description: Housing Law and Policy Clinic I. Students work under close faculty supervision on cases and  projects that involve the application of housing law and policy.

LAW 862.description: Housing Law and Policy. Introduce state and local housing law and policy with a focus on low-income tenants and undertake an exploration of current housing crisis.

LAW 863.description: International Negotiations and Mediation. Introduction to negotiation and mediation from an international  perspective.  Development of essential skills for effective client  representation in negotiation and mediation.  Open only to Law  students.

LAW 866.description: Counterterrorism, Privacy and Civil Liberties. Explores the spectrum of interrelated legal and policy issues known as "homeland security" since the events of September 11, 2001.

LAW 870.description: Legal Writing Fellows. Assist in teaching writing and advocacy. Responsibilities include helping prepare lesson plans and drafting writing assignments and sample answers; leading class exercises; and judging first-year moot court practice rounds. Graded CR/D/F.

LAW 871.description: First Amendment. Freedom of expression (political speech, symbolic expression, obscenity, commercial speech, defamation), rights of access to the media, religious protection and prohibition of establishment of religion.

LAW 879.description: Sports Law and Representation. Explores legal, ethical and business issues in sports, focusing on agent representation. Topics include contracts, collective bargaining, antitrust, NCAA compliance, NIL rules and labor relations.

LAW 884.description: Freedom and Oligarchy in the Constitution Seminar. Explores the ideas of freedom and oligarchy throughout US constitutional law through readings of caselaw, historical documents, political theory, and contemporary scholarship.

LAW 885.description: Major Trends in American Legal Thought. Major intellectual trends that have shaped both theory and  practice in American law since the twentieth century until the  present.

LAW 886.description: Intellectual Property Practicum. Providing supervised legal services to USC student films, mastering content clearance, contracts, risk analysis and client counseling within real-world entertainment production.

LAW 888.description: Negotiation Workshop. Introduces the theory and practice of negotiation, examining its stages and major tensions; distributive bargaining, value-creation, problem-solving techniques; communication, emotional elements, power dynamics, and ethics.

LAW 890.description: Directed Research. One CR/D/F unit for a research proposal approved by a full- or part-time faculty supervisor; up to four graded units with academic deans approval of proposal by LLM or third-year JD student to produce a publishable paper under full-time professor.

LAW 891.description: Post-Conviction Justice Project I. A year-long clinical program where second and third year students provide legal representation to men and women serving life terms in California prisons. Under faculty supervision  students represent clients on a variety of post-conviction matters, including parole hearings, state and federal habeas petitions, clemency applications and resentencing hearings and appeals. Experiential units.

LAW 893.description: Advanced Clinical Training. For third-year students who wish to continue their clinical  training.

LAW 894.description: Advanced Mediation Clinic. Students learn mediation skills, conduct live mediations and help to run the regular Mediation Clinic.

LAW 896.description: Stigma, Discrimination, and Mental Health Disorders. Examines the stigma against mental illness by and on behalf of the  U.S. government, with special attention to stigma within the  Department of Defense.

LAW 897.description: Justice in Education Practicum. Provides hands-on representation of students facing discrimination, disability, discipline, housing, and educational challenges while developing advocacy, litigation, and client-counseling skills.

LIM 500.description: Foundations of Library and Information Science. History and evolution of libraries and information organizations, including their structure, funding, role in society, and impact on the communities they serve.

LIM 502.description: User-Centered Collection Development. Collection development focused on the needs of patrons, in service of the institutional mission to serve and partner with the broader community.

LIM 503.description: Information Organization and Description for User Engagement. Theories, standards, and tools for the organization and description of information with the goal of equitable and inclusive access for users.

LIM 504.description: Social Science Research Methods in Library and Information S. Application of social science research methods in library and information science, including research question development, sampling, design methodologies, and data collection and analysis.

LIM 509.description: Information Sources and Services. Developments in reference and user services, including tools and processes for ethical information evaluation, retrieval and delivery for users in diverse library settings.

LIM 519.description: Leading Values-Driven Information Organizations. Effective application of interdisciplinary, community-centered leadership concepts in libraries and information organizations, with a focus on mission-driven, inclusive strategic planning and change management.

LIM 529.description: User Services and Community Engagement in Libraries. Investigation of various users and communities served by libraries and information organizations, and the development of programs and services tailored to their needs.

LIM 539.description: Project Management in Information Organizations. Practical applications for leadership and management in library and information organizations, with particular emphasis on project management concepts and methods.

LIM 541.description: Archives and Digital Curation. History and evolution of archival practice, and the strategies and tools needed for contemporary and future-facing archival management, preservation and digital curation.

LIM 549.description: Justice, Equity and Ethics in Information Organizations. History, theory and potential of social justice in library and information organizations, with the goal of implementing services and programs for diverse stakeholders.

LIM 562.description: Transformative Technologies in Library and Information Scien. Role of technology in libraries and information organizations, and potential use and ethical considerations of contemporary and emerging technologies to enhance library services.

LIM 598.description: Capstone in Library and Information Management. Knowledge and skills gained throughout the MMLIS program are synthesized in a culminating capstone project, and deployed in service of career advancement.

LING 107.description: Communication Disorders in Our Communities. Introduction to hearing disorders, motor speech disorders, and pragmatic disorders. The impact of these on effective communication. Common methods of diagnosing and intervening.

LING 110.description: In a Word. Words as tools for discovering properties of the human mind. How words are formed of and form various units. Experiments exploring judgments about word interpretation.

LING 115.description: Language and Society. Discourse patterns among diverse social groups in institutional and interpersonal settings; interrelationships among language practices and gender, socioeconomic status, ethnicity; social structures and cultural values as reflected in language policies and practices.

LING 120.description: American Sign Language I. Familiarization with ASL and fingerspelling. Covers visual and gestural communication, comprehension through receptive language skills, basic conversational proficiency, general insights into American Deaf culture.

LING 210.description: Introduction to Linguistics. Empirical study of the sounds and structures of human language;syntax and semantics; language change; linguistic universals.

LING 275.description: Language and Mind. Language within cognitive science: speech physiology and acoustics, language acquisition, reading, language disorders, perception and mental representation of words, linguistic diversity and computer analysis of speech.

LING 285.description: Human Language and Technology. Study of human linguistic competence and technologies that simulate it. Phonetics, vibration and signal processing, speech recognition, neural networks.

LING 302.description: Introduction to Syntax. A survey of topics in syntax.

LING 406.description: Psycholinguistics. Experimental and theoretical aspects of how spoken and written language is produced and understood, learned during childhood, and affected by brain damage.

LING 415.description: Phonetics. Familiarization with the articulation and transcription of speech  sounds.  Also vocal tract anatomy, acoustics, speech technology,  non-English sounds, perception.  Includes laboratory exercises.

LING 433.description: Children's Learning and Cognitive Development. Principles of learning and cognitive development from infancy through adolescence. Prerequisite 336.

LING 467.description: Language, Linguistics and Mind. Topics of current interest at the crossroads of philosophy of language, philosophy of mind and linguistics.

LING 486.description: Natural Language Processing. Introduction to modern neural network approaches to natural language processing, based on Deep Learning. Recursive and recurrent neural networks; backpropagation; Ngram models.

LING 490.description: Directed Research.  Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit.

LING 497.description: Honors Thesis.  Writing of the honors thesis. Registration is restricted to honors students.

LING 503.description: Professional Development I. Professional development for linguists in the early stages of their careers. Topics include funding, publishing, presenting work, and navigating available resources.

LING 504.description: Advanced Professional Development. Professional development in skills needed in disseminating and publishing dissertation work, developing undergraduate courses, supervising complex research projects, and navigating academia beyond the PhD.

LING 505C.description: Seminar in Linguistics. Colloquium for presentation and discussion of student research paper.
