CTPR 546.description: Production III, Fiction. An intensive workshop experience in which students, crewing in their area of specialization, complete the shooting and postproduction of projects up to 12 minutes in length. Qualifying courses: for directors, CTPR 532, and for cinematographers, CTPR 537;

CTPR 547.description: Production III, Documentary. Intensive workshop; students shoot and finish documentary projects up to about 25 minutes. Qualifying courses: for directors, CTPR 431 or CTPR 531; for cinematographers, CTPR 424 or CTPR 537.

CTPR 552.description: Advanced Directing. An advanced production class in directing. Encounters with         experienced directors; and individual student production of a      short. Recommended Preparation: CTPR 533.

CTPR 557.description: Advanced Cinematography. Advanced camera and lighting techniques for those considering a professional career in cinematography.

CTPR 558.description: Advanced Producing. Defines and examines the role of the Executive/Feature Producer through the preproduction, production and post production phases. Prerequisites: CTPR-538 or one of the following in equivalent crew position: CTPR 486, CTPR 546, CTPR 547.

CTPR 565.description: Making Media for Social Change. Each student will produce and direct a film incorporating a social issue of his/her choice into the narrative of the film. Prerequisites: CTPR 310 or CTPR 508.

CTPR 566.description: The Pitch Class: Film and TV. Developing, pitching and selling your feature motion picture and TV projects.

CTPR 572.description: The World of Television: From Concept to Air and Everything in Between. Takes projects from conception to sale, including development,  production, post-production, and marketing.  Students will develop  original projects.

CTPR 573.description: Developing and Producing the Advanced Project. An advanced preproduction workshop in which students complete the development and production planning of an advanced project to be executed in CTPR 581, CTPR 582 or CTPR 587a.

CTPR 581A.description: Individual Production Workshop. Individual experimental projects involving the creative use of visuals (live action or animated) and sound. Qualifying courses: CTPR 532 (for directors); CTPR 558 (for producers). Graded IP/Letter.

CTPR 581B.description: Individual Production Workshop. Individual experimental projects involving the creative use of visuals (live action or animated) and sound. Graded IP/Letter.

CTPR 581C.description: Individual Production Workshop. Individual experimental projects involving the creative use of visuals (live action or animated) and sound. Graded IP/Letter.

CTPR 581Z.description: Individual Production Workshop. Individual experimental projects involving the creative use of visuals (live action or animated) and sound. Graded IP/Letter.

CTPR 582A.description: Advanced Production Seminar. Advanced individual film or video projects under the guidance of a faculty mentor, without benefit of university equipment or resources. Qualifying courses: CTPR 532 (for directors); CTPR 558 (for producers). Graded IP/Letter.

CTPR 582B.description: Advanced Production Seminar. Advanced individual film or video projects under the guidance of a faculty mentor, without benefit of university equipment or resources. Graded IP/Letter.

CTPR 582Z.description: Advanced Production Seminar. Advanced individual film or video projects under the guidance of a faculty mentor, without benefit of university equipment or resources.  Open to Production students only.

CTPR 585A.description: Advanced Producing Project. Supervised, individual study leading to the creation of a producer's package. The package will include script, schedule, budget, finance and marketing plan. Graded IP/Letter.

CTPR 585B.description: Advanced Producing Project. Supervised, individual study leading to the creation of a producer's package. The package will include script, schedule, budget, finance and marketing plan. Graded IP/Letter.

CTPR 585Z.description: Advanced Producing Project. Supervised, individual study leading to the creation of a producer's package. The package will include script, schedule, budget, finance and marketing plan. Graded IP/Letter.

CTPR 587A.description: Group Production Workshop. Advanced group project involving the creative use of visuals (live action or animated) and sound specifically designed for students who want to work in pairs. Qualifying courses: CTPR 532 (for directors); CTPR 558 (for producers).

CTPR 587B.description: Group Production Workshop. Advanced group project involving the creative use of visuals (live action or animated) and sound specifically designed for students who want to work in pairs.

CTPR 587C.description: Group Production Workshop. Advanced group project involving the creative use of visuals (live action or animated) and sound specifically designed for students who want to work in pairs.

CTPR 587Z.description: Group Production Workshop. Advanced group project involving the creative use of visuals (live action or animated) and sound specifically designed for students who want to work in pairs.

PJMT 500.description: Principles of Project Management. Concepts including delivering project scope within cost, schedule, and resource constraints and the exploration of the traditional or waterfall project management methodology will be explored.

PJMT 505.description: Requirements Elicitation and Business Analysis. Tasks, techniques, and perspectives on how to approach business analysis along with methods for developing requirement process tools and techniques and best practices.

PJMT 510.description: Schedule Management. Structured approach to project schedule management, demonstrating how to be proactive and in control of projects by implementing effective schedule management.

PJMT 515.description: Cost Estimation and Forecasting. Approaches to project cost estimation and the tools and methodologies best suited for estimates and forecasts that need to be prepared.

PJMT 520.description: Risk Management. Coursework will enable students to prepare a comprehensive risk management plan and discover different approaches to identify, assess, and quantify risks and their impacts.

PJMT 525.description: Agile Project Management Methodologies. Agile project management concepts and a set of frameworks that covers the people, products, and techniques required to successfully implement projects.

PJMT 530.description: Quality and Process Improvement. Quality and performance improvement projects and methodologies used to implement them with a focus on Six Sigma, Lean, and Total Quality Management.

PJMT 535.description: Specialized Project Management. Explores several industries and entities and their developed project management methodologies to meet industry-specific needs through traditional approaches and partnerships in various sectors.

PJMT 540.description: Organizational Change Management and Business Relationships. Students learn to cultivate the necessary components for stakeholder management on nearly any change within an organization through change management and business relationship management.

PJMT 545.description: Program Management. Managing and coordinating multiple organizational projects with a focus on project alignment, organizational goals, performance maximization, risk minimization, and program success.

PJMT 550.description: Portfolio Management. Structured approach to design, build, and manage a project portfolio, focusing on strategic implementation and operational initiatives to create sustainable value.

PJMT 555.description: Project Management Capstone. Utilize skills gained throughout the program to demonstrate the ability to plan and implement a project from conception to conclusion.

PBHS 301.description: Science and Practice of Building Resilience. Promotes learning principles and skills that enhance resilience to effectively navigate common stressors throughout a professional career through course lecture, group discussion, reflection and practice.

PBHS 490.description: Directed Research. Individual research and readings.

PSYC 100.description: Introduction to Psychology. Introduction to psychological science, including historical and contemporary approaches. Behavior examined from biological, cognitive, social, developmental, and personality perspectives. Disorders and treatments.

PSYC 274.description: Statistics. Introduction to the use of statistics in psychology: basic ideas in measurement; frequency distributions; descriptive statistics; concepts and procedures in statistical inference.

PSYC 290.description: Supervised Research in Psychology. Supervised Research with department faculty.

PSYC 301.description: Cognitive Processes.  Experimental and theoretical aspects of human memory, perception, thinking, and language. Lectures, demonstrations, and individual experiments. Prerequisite: 100g or departmental approval.

PSYC 304.description: Sensation and Perception.  Receptor processes and stimulus organization; traditional topics  in the perception of objects, space, time. Laboratory              demonstrations and exercises.

PSYC 305.description: Learning and Memory.  Principles involved in classical and operant conditioning.        Concentration on basic causes of behavior; consideration of the    relevance of simple behavioral laws to complicated human behavior.

PSYC 314.description: Experimental Research Methods. Experimental research methods in psychology; nature and concepts of scientific method.

PSYC 316.description: Non-Experimental Research Methods . Non-experimental research methods in psychology. Observational, survey and data analysis exercises

PSYC 320.description: Principles of Psychobiology. The integrative study of bio-behavioral systems. Evolutionary, developmental, ecological, social, ethological, and physiological factors mediating representative behavioral and psychological phenomenon are examined in detail.

PSYC 326.description: Behavioral Neuroscience. Neural bases of behavior. Concentration on sensory and motor processes and the interaction of neural, chemical, and hormonal systems.

PSYC 336.description: Developmental Psychology.  Child and adolescent behavior and associated theories;            exploration of the continuity between child and adult behavior.    Laboratory projects.

PSYC 339.description: Origins of the Mind. Exploration of ancient philosophical questions concerning the origins of human knowledge through empirical studies of infants, animals, and adults from diverse cultures.

PSYC 353.description: Close Relationships. Scientific perspective of close relationships: intimate relationships, friendships and others, evolutionary and biological bases of attraction and love, historical, social , cultural influences. Prerequisite: PSYC 100. (Duplicates credit in PSYC 359)

PSYC 355.description: Social Psychology.  Theoretical and experimental analysis of human behavior. Social   processes involved in attitudes, conformity, compliance,           interpersonal perception, liking, affiliation, aggression,         altruism, and group dynamics.

PSYC 357.description: Psychology of Persuasion. A critical analysis of persuasion used to influence individuals and groups using social media and artificial intelligence based on psychological scientific theories and methods.

PSYC 360.description: Psychological Disorders. The commonly diagnosed behavior pathologies; biological, social, cultural and developmental antecedents of abnormal behavior; principles of learning, perception and motivation, as they relate to psychopathology.

PSYC 361.description: Introduction to Clinical Psychology. Introduction to the scientist-practitioner model of clinical psychology, including research methods, psychological assessment and diagnosis, psychotherapeutic interventions, and treatment of special populations.

PSYC 363.description: Criminal Behavior. Genetic, biological, psychological, and sociological characteristics of those who evidence criminal behavior; theoretical formulations to be reviewed and appraised. Prerequisites: PSYC 100. Duplicates credit in former PSYC 463.

PSYC 367.description: Stress, Health, and the Mind-Body Connection. Introduction to psychological, biological and behavioral processes affecting physical health, including stress, coping with disease, health behaviors and socioeconomic and cultural influences on health.

PSYC 375.description: States of Consciousness: From Dreams to Drugs. The psychological science of states consciousness including sleep, animal and machine consciousness, and altered states of consciousness as a result of drugs, meditation and hypnosis.

PSYC 422.description: Human Judgment and Decision Making. Descriptive and normative models of decision making; topics  include probability judgments, inference, correlation, emotion,  mental accounting, decision analysis, lens model, equity, social  dilemmas, time, risk.

PSYC 426.description: Motivated Behaviors and Addiction. Social, environmental, and physiological influences on behaviors associated with aggression, eating, reproduction, and sleep. Will focus on behavioral disorders such as addiction.

PSYC 434.description: Intelligence, Problem Solving and Creativity . Psychometric and experimental approaches to the study of  intelligence, problem solving, reasoning and creativity, including  analysis of mental test construction and validity.

PSYC 436.description: Developmental Neuroscience of Human Behavior. The biological underpinnings supporting social, emotional, and cognitive development from infancy through adolescence; Focus on neuroscience to understand typical and atypical development, including psychopathology.

PSYC 437.description: Adolescent Development. The adolescent years from both an applied and a research-oriented perspective. Topics include physical, cognitive, and moral development; socialization; and sexual and sex-role development.

PSYC 439.description: Science of Yoga and Meditation. Reviews intersection between modern science and ancient contemplative practices of yoga and meditation. Explores mind-body-spirit connection through personal practice, review of contemplative texts and empirical research.

PSYC 450.description: Neural Network Models of Social and Cognitive Processes. Introduction to using neural network or connectionist models to simulate cognitive, social, emotional and motivational processes; basic concepts and tools in computational neuroscience.

PSYC 452.description: Social Neuroscience. Overview of principles and research in social neuroscience, which uses neuroscience approaches to inform social processes including empathy, inter-group relations, emotion, morality and social decision-making.

PSYC 454.description: Social Cognition.  Theory and research on cognitive processes in social behavior, to include social inference, cognition and emotion, the Self, social  categorization, person memory, and attribution processes.  Recommended preparation: PSYC-355.

PSYC 459.description: Industrial/Organizational Psychology. I/O Psychologists develop and apply scientifically supported solutions to the workplace. "Industrial" deals with human resource functions, and "Organizational" with psychological aspects of the organization. Prerequisite: PSYC 100. Recommended preparation: PSYC 316.

PSYC 464.description: Psychology of Marriage and the Family. Theories and research on family relationships across the life  span, including research methods, cultural and developmental  perspectives, communication, conflict, attachment, individual  psychopathology, and family violence.

PSYC 467.description: Introduction to Autism Spectrum Disorder. A comprehensive overview of the assessment, diagnosis and treatment of individuals diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder.

PSYC 468.description: Happiness:  Research in Neuroscience and Positive Psychology. Neuroscientific and psychological perspectives that investigate the basis of happiness and well-being.

PSYC 490.description: Directed Research.  Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit.

PSYC 499.description: Special Topics. Selected topics in the various specialty areas within psychology.  Topic will vary from semester to semester.

PSYC 505.description: Research Methods in Applied Social Psychology. Various research techniques that are useful in a variety of different real world settings, such as business, governmental agencies and charities. Open only to M.S., Applied Psychology students.

PSYC 509.description: Qualitative Research Methods in Applied Psychology. Examines qualitative research in applied settings. Learn to design, execute and report qualitative research in response to stakeholder needs.

PSYC 514.description: Psychopathology. Study of psychopathology: in-depth survey of theory and research concerning psychological disorders; introduction to diagnosis. (One of 4 clinical psychology core courses: 514, 515, 619, 620.)

PSYC 515.description: Clinical Assessment. Study of clinical assessment: test construction, measurement and predicition of behavior, major cognitive and personality assessment instruments. (One of 4 clinical psychology core courses: 514, 515, 619, 620.)

PSYC 517.description: Group Dynamics and Leadership. Theory and research on effective teams and characteristics of strong leaders. Negotiation, morale-building, managing expectancies, utilization of cultural diversity as a strength. Open only to M.S., Applied Psychology students.

PSYC 519.description: Professional Issues for Clinical Scientists. Focus is on professionalism topics and skills central to developing as a clinical scientist, explored within a cultural context.

PSYC 521.description: Cross Cultural Psychology in Applied Settings. Examination of major theoretical frameworks mapping worldwide cultures and values with a focus on applying thatknowledge in organizations. Open only to master students in Applied Psychology.

PSYC 523.description: User Experience (UX) Research. Provides a broad introduction to the social science methods UX researchers most commonly use, including qualitative approaches, and quantitative approaches.

PSYC 530.description: Concepts and Principles of Behavior Analysis. Provides intensive training in behavioral principles and laws of learning and motivation. Focuses on broad application of principles, from basic research with nonhumans, to application across human clinical populations.

PSYC 531.description: Behavioral Assessment. Studies theory and application of behavioral methods for skill assessment, functional assessment of destructive behavior, and learner motivation. Discusses relative strengths and limitations of direct versus indirect methods.

PSYC 532.description: Ethics for Behavior Analysts. Provides training in legal and ethical issues as they pertain to the professional practice of behavior analysis. Reviews the Guidelines for Responsible Conduct for Behavior Analysts, as well as the American Psychological Associations Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct.

PSYC 533.description: Applied Developmental Psychology. Review of theories of cognitive development. Analysis of research on brain functioning, perception, memory, language, reasoning and academic skills from birth to adolescence.

PSYC 534.description: Social and Emotional Development in Children. Theories of social and emotional development, including sociocultural perspectives.  Analysis of research on temperament,  social relationships, individuation and moral development from  birth to adolescence.  Open to graduate students in psychology.

PSYC 547.description: Functional Neuroanatomy. Regional organization and systems of the mammalian nervous system and their functions.

PSYC 550A.description: Proseminar in Human Behavior. The nature of the human mind, social interactions, conflicts, cooperative behavior, mutual influence and effectiveness. Application of psychological principles to the dynamics of commercial entities. Open only to M.S., Applied Psychology students.

PSYC 552.description: Principles of Consumer Psychology. Examination of the attitudes and decisions of consumers, and how to effectively reach consumers by using persuasion and proper positioning in the marketplace. Open only to M.S., Applied Psychology students.

PSYC 556.description: Psychology of Interactive Media. Examination of the diverse methods of communicating with a target audience with a special emphasis on the newest computer-based tools for providing information and influence.

PSYC 565.description: Organizational Psychology. Examination of the psychological factors that impact employee motivation, job satisfaction, teamwork, leadership, and organizational development. Open only to Master of Applied Psychology students. Not available for major credit for GSBA majors

PSYC 571.description: Foundations of Statistical and Data Analytic     Methods in Psychology                           . Model comparison approach to analyzing experimental and non-experimental data; including moderated, mediated and nonlinear models as well as models with a categorical outcome.

PSYC 580.description: Applied Research Design. Supports students on their capstone treatise, allowing them to consider topics, ideate on research design, develop a proposal and draft a treatise protocol.

PSYC 587.description: Practicum in Applied Behavior Analysis. Provides supervised practical experience in implementing behavior analytic assessment and treatment services. Meets supervision requirements for the Board Certified Behavior Analyst exam. Students meet with course instructor to present and discuss cases for two hours per week every semester, including one summer session. Practicum hours in the field vary from 18-20 hours per week during the academic year to 30 hours per week during the summer.

PSYC 588.description: Capstone Project in Behavior Analysis. Supervision for completing independent project, consisting of practical treatment evaluation, program development, or literature review.

PSYC 590.description: Directed Research.  Research leading to the master's degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

PSYC 591.description: Applied Psychology Internship. Internship in a non-university setting, such as business, governmental agency, or NGO. Graded CR/NC. Open only to M.S., Applied Psychology students.

PSYC 592.description: Applied Psychology Treatise. Requires a research paper of substantial length and high quality that integrates the Internship experience with concepts and principles of human behavior. Credit/No Credit. Open only to M.S., Applied Psychology students.

PSYC 593.description: Practicum in Teaching Psychology. Techniques for working with undergraduates, lesson planning, leading discussions and lecturing, tools for development as a teaching professional. Open to first-semester Psychology TAs only. Graded CR/NC.

PSYC 594A.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of Thesis. Graded CR/NC.

PSYC 594B.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of Thesis. Graded CR/NC.

PSYC 594Z.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of Thesis. Graded CR/NC.

PSYC 595.description: Practicum in Clinical Psychology. Supervised experience in interviewing skills and in assessment, including psychological test administration, and the preparation of reports. Graded CR/NC.

PSYC 596.description: Advanced Behavioral Theory. Examines advanced topics in behavioral theory and philosophy, including a comprehensive behavioral approach to language and cognition. Discusses the nature of productive relations between behavior analysis and other psychological theories.

PSYC 597.description: Internship for Curricular Practical Training. Part-time or full-time, practical work experience in the students field of study. The internship must be located at an off-campus facility. Students are individually supervised by faculty. May not be taken until the student has completed at least two semesters of enrollment in the graduate program.

PSYC 599.description: Special Topics. Selected topics in the various specialty areas within psychology at the graduate level. Topic will vary from semester to semester.

PSYC 621.description: Seminar in Quantitative Psychology.  Selected topics in mathematical psychology.

PSYC 622.description: Decision Analysis and Behavioral Decision Theory.  Normative and descriptive theories and research on human decision-making, with special emphasis on applications to real social decision problems.

PSYC 660.description: Seminar in Clinical Psychology.  Selected topics in clinical psychology.

PSYC 691A.description: Internship in Clinical Psychology.  Supervised clinical work in an approved mental health setting. Graded CR/NC. Prerequisite: Good standing in clinical program and departmental approval.

PSYC 695.description: Advanced Practicum in Clinical Psychology. Didactic practicum combining theory and research on psychological intervention with clinical practice in assessment and treatment, focused on particular client groups or disorders. Graded CR/NC.

PSYC 696.description: Externship for Practical Training. Externship for Practical Training is for clinical-related training experience in the students fieldof study. Students are individually supervised at their site.

PSYC 790.description: Research.  Research leading to the doctorate. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

PSYC 794A.description: Doctoral Dissertation. Credit on acceptance of Dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC.

PSYC 794B.description: Doctoral Dissertation. Credit on acceptance of Dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC.

PSYC 794C.description: Doctoral Dissertation.  Credit on acceptance of Dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC.

PSYC 794D.description: Doctoral Dissertation.  Credit on acceptance of Dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC.

PSYC 794Z.description: Doctoral Dissertation. Credit on acceptance of Dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC.

PUBD 502.description: Historical and Comparative Approaches to Public Diplomacy. Examines historical and comparative approaches to public  diplomacy.  Explores public diplomacy operations in public and  private settings, by individuals and institutions.  Reviews  traditional, critical, war, and peace perspectives.

PUBD 504.description: Global Issues and Public Diplomacy. Focuses on critical global issues/challenges that require some  form of intervention from the international community.  Taught  with active leading strategies: case studies and "problem-based  learning."

PUBD 511.description: Race and Public Diplomacy. Examines the impact of race and racism on U.S. foreign policy generally and public diplomacy specifically.

PUBD 590.description: Directed Research. Research leading to the master's degree.  Maximum units which may  be applied to the degree to be determined by the school.  Graded  CR/NC.

PUBD 596.description: Practicum in Public Diplomacy Research         . Development and production of original research-based project in  the area of public diplomacy.  Graded CR/NC.

PR 209.description: Effective Writing for Strategic Public Relations and Adverti. Focus on the unique writing requirements of social, online, broadcast, print and other media in public relations/advertising; emphasis on judgment, context and audience understanding. Non-majors who are interested in enrolling must have at least a 2.5 GPA.

PR 250.description: Strategic Public Relations and Advertising: An Introduction. Strategies/practices in the growing field of public relations and advertising, including landmark cases, campaign planning; special emphasis on historical roots, current and future practice.

PR 340.description: Introduction to Advertising. History and development of advertising; basic advertising campaigns showing relationships of marketing, creative, print and electronic media.

PR 351A.description: Multichannel Strategy and Content Creation. Introduction to media relations, social media and influencer engagement; intensive writing and creating multimedia content for traditional, emerging and social media.

PR 400.description: Practicum for PR Media Center. A hands-on learning lab, exploring how to create original social media content while adhering to media production cycle.

PR 427.description: Structured Inquiry in Public Relations and Advertising. Apply contemporary research methods to create actionable insights for integrated, multi-channel communication campaigns, including social media monitoring, measurement and evaluation.

PR 429.description: Business and Economic Foundations of Public Relations and Ad. Relationship between public relations/advertising and other organizational disciplines; understanding business goals and objectives; economic literacy; financial/investor relations; how PR/communication agencies are built and managed.

PR 432.description: Concepting: Advertising Strategy and Creative Development. Learn how to develop an idea and transform that idea to create advertisements that cut through the clutter and communicate persuasively.

PR 433.description: Advertising and Technology. Hands-on introduction to advertising's digital tools, platforms, media, channels and techniques through an insider's view of LA's technology companies.

PR 444.description: Lifestyle Public Relations. An extensive overview of the Lifestyle Public Relations category with special emphasis on social media, non-traditional influencers and audience segmentation.

PR 445.description: Fundamentals of Food Communication. Examines the role of food, food-related communication and media in our daily lives, our various cultures and our local, national and global economy.

PR 450.description: Building Integrated Campaigns. In-depth study of methods for planning, managing and evaluating strategic communication campaigns; critical analysis of contemporary cases; development of campaigns for real world clients.

PR 452.description: Public Relations in Entertainment. Public relations in the design, promotion, and presentation of popular entertainment, including films, broadcasting, music, expositions, amusement parks, resorts and arenas.

PR 453.description: Public Relations Strategies for Working with Athletes. Sports Public Relations isn't only getting press for a team or player; it's managing communications among influencers. Complements overview course giving students advanced look at practitioners' role with professional athletes.

PR 454.description: Sports Public Relations. Introduction to the field of sports information and promotion, including lectures, media assignments, role-playing, and presentations by sports professionals.

PR 455.description: Public Relations for Non-Profit Organizations. Introduction to the specialized field of public relations for non-profit and non-governmental organizations; emphasis on case studies, strategic and critical thinking, and campaign development.

PR 457.description: The Role of Celebrity in Public Relations. Understanding of the history and application of celebrity in public relations, focusing on the entertainment industry and the notoriety attached to politics and the media.

PR 458.description: Political Public Relations and Advocacy. Application of public relations principles to the context of political campaigns; emphasis on message development and delivery; relationship between candidate, news media, and electorate.

PR 478.description: Social Media Analytics: Data, Content Creation and Campaign . Application of monitoring tools to become social media analysts and real-time content creators; interpretation of large data sets drawn from the social web; understanding of how to present data visually for optimal impact.

PR 486.description: Multimedia PR Content: Introduction to Digital Design Tools. Hands-on lab; producing multimedia content; basic principles of design; tools and techniques to create digital images and layouts.

PR 487.description: Multimedia PR Content: Introduction to Audio/Video Tools. Hands-on lab; audio/video tools for conceiving, shooting, editing, delivering and archiving compelling stories for online audiences; personal brand building; digital storytelling trends and applications.

PR 488.description: Multimedia PR Content: Visual Communication of   Information                                     . Overview of tools and techniques available to convey messages and experiences; exploration into graphic design, visual branding, design methods and processes.

PR 490.description: Directed Research. Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit.

PR 499.description: Special Topics. Selected topics in public relations.

PR 508.description: Public Relations and Advertising Fundamentals and Strategy. Explores the practice of public relations and advertising in a broader strategic communication and digital context; emphasizing strategy, critical thinking and problem solving.

PR 522.description: Storytelling with Data Intelligence. Provides the foundations of quantitative research methods, the basics of storytelling with data and critical thinking skills in public relations, advertising and related fields.

PR 523.description: Advanced Audience Insight Mining. Provides student training with cutting-edge digital research methods and applied data analytic skills relevant to current and future public relations and advertising practices.

PR 525.description: Multimedia Content Creation for Brand Storytelling II. Conceptualization and creation of strategic, research-based, primarily image and video multimedia content for use by organizations of all types.

PR 535.description: Persuasive Writing. Teaches persuasive writing for practitioners in public relations, advertising, influencer relations and brand activation  through in-class writing drills with and without deadline pressure.

PR 537.description: Public Relations and Branding. Concept of branding, including brand definition, brand engagement, brand management and the role of public relations in creating brand value.

PR 540.description: Branding through Partnerships, Activations and Influencers. Analyze celebrity partnerships, influencer campaigns and brand integrations. Create innovative entertainment marketing strategies across media platforms. Evaluate ROI and risk management.

PR 565.description: Corporate Public Relations and Reputation. Learn all aspects of corporate communications and reputation management through real-time news analysis, cases and senior guest speakers from the world's largest, most admired companies.

PR 590.description: Directed Research. Research leading to the master's degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department.

PR 594A.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of thesis.

PR 594Z.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of thesis.

PR 598.description: Improvisational Leadership. Leadership workshop inspires stepping outside of comfort zones to be braver and more creative.  Encourages discovery of leadership potential by exploring new ideas and challenges.

PRSM 500.description: Strategic Planning for Multichannel Communication Campaigns. Explores the contemporary practices of branding, advertising and public relations, and their expanding role in the development of multichannel communication campaign plans.

PRSM 505.description: Data-Driven Brand Storytelling. Explores the evaluation of research and analysis methods, generating data insights and creating compelling and accurate stories using data visualization techniques.

PRSM 510.description: Leadership and Ethics for Communication Practitioners. Explores the leadership skills and ethics required in todays complex organizations, communication with key stakeholders, creative problem solving and promoting diversity, equity, inclusion and access.

PRSM 515.description: Business and Economic Literacy for Communicators. Covers fundamental business, finance and economics knowledge needed to better align the communication function with organizational goals and communicate effectively with key stakeholders.

PRSM 520.description: Multiplatform Content Creation I. Introduces brand storytelling through the creation of content across multiple channels and platforms using applicable tools, focusing on design and layout.

PRSM 525.description: Multiplatform Content Creation II. Covers brand storytelling through the creation of content across multiple channels and platforms using applicable tools, with a focus on image, audio and video elements.

PRSM 530.description: Employee Communication. Explores employee communication strategies, tools and channels used to engage employees and develop them as brand advocates in support of organizational purpose and goals.

PRSM 535.description: Social Media Advertising. Covers the development of comprehensive social media advertising strategies that maximize budgets, ethically target their audiences and meet the goals of communication campaigns.

PRSM 550.description: Brand Purpose Communication. Explores best practices for brand communication, social issue engagement and advocacy, value alignment, guiding stakeholders on purpose communication and planning purpose-led campaigns or projects.

PRSM 555.description: Emerging Game-Changers for Communication Practitioners. Explores impacts of emerging technologies, innovation and organizational culture concepts and the centrality of emerging technologies in shaping the digital future.

QBIO 305.description: Statistics for Biological Sciences. Statistical methods in biological science and medicine, including populations and samples, random sampling, confidence intervals, paired samples and regression.

QBIO 460.description: Introduction to Machine Learning in Biology. Fundamentals of ML; regression analysis, classification methods, clustering techniques; dimensionality reduction methods, ensemble learning and deep learning technologies; applications in various biological contexts; project-based.

QBIO 475.description: Statistical and Evolutionary Genetics. Introduction to the mathematical modeling and statistical analysis of genetic variation, including genetic drift, natural selection, mutation, migration, population structure, family studies and GWAS.

QBIO 481.description: Structural Bioinformatics: From Atoms to Cells. Introduction to physical and statistical methods, molecular simulations, machine learning and AI for structural bioinformatics studies of proteins, nucleic acids, molecular complexes and whole cells.

QBIO 490.description: Directed Research. Individual research and readings. Project approval by  faculty adviser and QCB department required.

QBIO 493.description: Quantitative Biology Honors Seminar. Student-led discussions of recent research in quantitative biology and presentation of their own research.

QBIO 540.description: Probability and Statistics for Computational Sciences. Graduate-level introduction to probability theory and mathematical statistics for students in the sciences and engineering, with examples largely from biology.

QBIO 542.description: Seminar in Computational Biology. Experience and training in giving science research presentations. Students will discuss recent research in computational biology and bioinformatics.

QBIO 547.description: Ethics and Professional Conduct in Computational Biology. Discussion-based ethics course for graduate students, with topics including authorship, peer review, publication, research misconduct, discrimination in science, data privacy and algorithmic bias.

QBIO 570.description: Introduction to Data Structures and Algorithms for Science. An introduction to scientific data analysis; fundamentals of data structures and algorithms; specialized algorithms used in the sciences; challenges posed by large scientific data sets.

QBIO 590.description: Directed Research. Research leading to a graduate degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

QBIO 593.description: Practicum in Teaching Quantitative and Computational Biology. Practical principles for the long-term development of effective teaching within science and engineering disciplines. Intended for teaching assistant training as required by the university.

QBIO 596.description: Internship for Curricular Practical Training. Part-time or full-time, practical work experience in the student's field of study. The internship must be located at an off-campus facility. Students are supervised by faculty. May not be taken until the student has completed one semester of enrollment in a graduate program with a cumulative 3.0 GPA. The course is graded CR/NC.

QBIO 790.description: Research. Research leading to the doctorate. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

QBIO 794B.description: Doctoral Dissertation. For doctoral students who have passed the qualifying exam. Credit on acceptance of dissertation.

RED 200.description: Introduction to Real Estate. Basic understanding of the real estate industry, the process of real estate development and investment, and the key players involved.

RED 201.description: Real Estate Career Seminar. Career assessment and preparation; real estate industry overview; reflection on experiences.

RED 301.description: Real Estate Internship Seminar. Real estate development skills for practice; internship seminar; leadership, group dynamics and presentation skills; application of management; organizational diversity; reflection on experiences.

RED 325.description: Introduction to Finance in Cities. Basic understanding of public finance, public debt, public-private joint ventures, time value of money, present value, risk and return, discounted cash flows, leverage and taxes.

RED 351.description: Land Use Regulation. Land use planning and zoning; community and government relations; environmental regulation.

RED 362.description: Real Estate Development Fundamentals. Real estate overview; evolution of cities and neighborhoods; product types; introduction to valuation.

RED 375.description: Real Estate Development Analysis. Real estate development feasibility and analysis; underwriting local fundamentals including neighborhood and city change, real estate capital flows.

RED 398.description: Shaping Cities Through Real Estate. Cities and urban form created through various real estate product types. Case studies and site visits.

RED 417.description: History of Planning and Development. Historical evolution of planning and development. How changing modes of planning and development have shaped the built landscape throughout the century.

RED 425.description: Designing Livable Communities. Theories and concepts of livable communities and good city form; case studies of historical and current best practices; field visits; collaborative design project.

RED 435.description: Analyzing Real Estate Markets. Macro and micro-analysis of urban property markets; demographics; location choice; regulation.

RED 437.description: Advanced Finance and Investment for Real Estate  Development                                     . Advanced real estate principles. Underwriting property valuation and deal structure including risk and return. Debt and equity markets; difference between development and existing assets.

RED 490.description: Directed Research. Individual research and readings.

RED 509.description: Market Analysis for Real Estate. Explores macro and micro aspects of residential, retail, office,  and industrial markets and examines methodologies for analyzing  such markets for real estate development/investment purposes.

RED 510.description: Real Estate Practice and Principles. Fundamental principles of real estate analysis; economics; capital markets; development decision making; relationships between real estate markets and federal, state and local government policies; property value.

RED 511.description: Foundations of Real Estate Analysis. Principles of real estate analysis; captial markets; importance of uncertainty and metrics of risk; investments; valuation techniques; use of debty and equity, leases, taxes;

RED 542.description: Finance of Real Estate Development. Theory and methods of real estate finance and investment. Real estate investment analysis, real estate entities, taxation; introduction to securization of real estate equities, debt.

RED 544.description: Real Estate Capital Markets. Explore structure, instruments and institutions of real estate  capital markets.  Consider linkages between real estate and  capital markets.  Asses role of Real Estate Investment Trusts.

RED 562.description: Legal Issues in Real Estate Development. Ownership and transfer of real estate; formation and enforcement  of contracts; business associations; environmental regulation;  taxation of property transfers; acquiring, financing, leasing of  commercial property.

RED 563.description: Introduction to the Asset Management of Real Estate. Overview of institutional asset management: creating and  implementing investment and portfolio strategies through the  development, acquisition, underwriting, and operational stages of  the investment, asset disposition.

RED 574.description: Building Typologies. The exploration of categories of building types, including retail, industrial, residential, office, and institutional, using key examples or case studies from each.

RED 590.description: Directed Research. Research leading to the master's degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

RED 598.description: Real Estate Product Development. An evaluation of various real estate development product types. Case studies and site visits.

RNR 050.description: International Academy Holding Course . Course created per request from the International Academy to  create a zero unit, zero charge course for the purpose of enabling  services for the student  population.  Tuition is paid directly to  the Academy.

RNR 051.description: International Academy Holding Course (Part II). Course created per request from the International Academy to  create a zero unit, zero charge course for the purpose of enabling  services for the student population. This course serves the  popuation that has successfully completed RNR-050.  Tuition is  paid directly to the Academy.

RSCI 506.description: Auditing Principles. Audit requirements mandated by the FDA and other international regulatory agencies, including internal, external, regulatory agency, third party, GMP, GLP, ISO 13485/QSR and supplier audits.

RSCI 510.description: Statistical Process Control and Lean Manufacturing. Course explores SPC, Lean Manufacturing, and Process Analytical Technology to build efficient, compliant medical product manufacturing processes, emphasizing real-time monitoring, statistical methods, and continuous improvement.

lectures.instructor: Gopal Mohanty; Eunjoo Pacifici; Susan Bain

RSCI 511.description: Introduction to Medical Product Regulation. Introduction to regulatory environments surrounding medical product development, manufacturing and marketing; operation of federal, state and international regulatory bodies.

RSCI 512.description: Regulation of Pharmaceutical and Biological Products. Ensuring safety and effectiveness of new drugs and biologics; marketing and monitoring approved pharmaceutical/biological products; management of genetically engineered products.

RSCI 513.description: Regulation of Medical Devices and Diagnostics. Development and testing of new medical products according to U.S. and international regulatory requirements.

lectures.instructor: Gopal Mohanty; Eunjoo Pacifici; Susan Bain

RSCI 516.description: Medical Products and the Law. Legal issues affecting intellectual property, medical product development, marketing and safety, taught through case studies and lectures.

RSCI 517.description: Structure and Management of Clinical Trials. Development and execution of clinical trials: bioethical principles, good clinical practices, project management and documentation.

RSCI 518.description: Writing Regulatory Drug Submissions. Developing form and content for investigational drug applications, new drug applications, biologic licensing applications to FDA; common technical documents; considerations of writing style.

RSCI 521.description: Seminars in Regulatory Science. Current problems in regulatory affairs, legal management, preclinical and clinical testing, scientific evaluation and quality assurance. (Duplicates credit in former MPTX 521.) Graded CR/NC. Recommended preparation: undergraduate degree in pharmacy, medical or independent health sciences, engineering or equivalent mix of post secondary training and industry experience; enrollment in MS Regulatory Science program.

RSCI 526.description: Chemistry Manufacturing and Controls. Provides a firm foundation in the domestic and international CMC process, from concept to commercialization of new active pharmaceutical ingredients and products.

RSCI 533.description: Safety Evaluation during Drug Development. Safety pharmacology/toxicology requirements mandated by FDA and other regulatory agencies to move a new chemical entity from discovery stage to market approval

RSCI 536.description: Clinical Trial Writing and Documentation Management. Clinical Trials management and operations are vital aspects in the design, planning, conduct and reporting of successful research projects and portfolios.

RSCI 543.description: Team-based Regulatory and Quality Solutions (TRAQS). Experiential learning via working in teams on real-time regulatory, clinical, or quality healthcare issues with sponsors and DRQS faculty supervision.

RSCI 590.description: Directed Research. Research leading to the master's degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

RSCI 596.description: Internship for Curricular Practical Training in  Regulatory Science                              . Part-time or full-time practical work experience in Regulatory Science. The internship must be located at an off-campus facility. Students are individually supervised by faculty. Graded CR/NC. Recommended preparation: Undergraduate or professional degree in pharmacy, medicine or independent health sciences, engineering or equivalent mix of post-secondary training and industry experience; enrollment in MS (Regulatory Science).

RSCI 605.description: Managing Organizations and Human Resources. Theory and practice of personnel management, organizational  structure and industrial relations in small, growing enterprises  and large global companies typical of pharmaceutical and medical  device sectors  Recommended Preparation: Undergraduate or  professional degree in pharmacy, medical or independent health  sciences, engineering or equivalent mix of post-secondary training  and industry experience.

RSCI 630.description: Directed Field-Research Project. Research/policy analysis conducted under preceptor supervision in an industrial or governmental setting.

RSCI 790.description: Directed Research. Research leading to the doctorate. Maximum units which may be applied towards the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC

RSCI 794A.description: Doctoral Dissertation. Dissertation research required for completion of doctoral degree  in Regulatory Science.

RSCI 794B.description: Doctoral Dissertation. Dissertation research required for completion of doctoral degree  in Regulatory Science.

REL 130.description: Indian Traditions of Mind and Body. Explores a variety of sophisticated theories and practices from India relating to the mind, body, medicine and religion.

REL 137.description: Introduction to Islam. Introduction to Islam, emphasizing its historical and cultural development since the seventh century C.E., and the basic teachings of Islam.

REL 301.description: Approaches to the Study of Religion. Survey of academic approaches to the study of religion. When possible this course will be taken during the first year of the major or minor.

REL 322.description: Religion and Science. Explores whether religion and science offer competing or complementary models for understanding the world and the human place within it.

REL 327.description: Heretics, Martyrs, and Miracles. Examines Christianity in the second century including theology, ethics and identity.

REL 345.description: Islamic Spirituality: Mysticism and the Sufi Tradition. Examination of the origins, development, and basic concepts and practices of Sufism, as well as its relationship to other areas of Islamic life.

REL 361.description: Law and Religion. Explores the intersection between law and religion including ways in which religious traditions conceive of, create, order, and contest law.

REL 462.description: Religion and Violence. Religious and moral perspectives on war, pacifism, violent and non-violent protest, and religion-based terrorism and militia.

REL 490.description: Directed Research.  Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit.

REL 491.description: Undergraduate Honors Research. Individual research for honors in the major leading to a  substantial project.

REL 500.description: Methods and Theories in the Study of Religion.  Introduction to the major topics, trends, and theoretical approaches in the study of religion.

REL 535.description: Colloquium in Christian Studies. Research methods and recent scholarship in Christian Studies.

REL 545.description: Colloquium in Asia Pacific Religions. Research methods, tools and current scholarship in the study of Asian Pacific Religions.

REL 590.description: Directed Research.  Research leading to the master's degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

REL 650.description: Readings in Islamic Texts. Study of Islamic religious texts in multiple genres, primarily in Arabic, though other languages may be offered. Recommended preparation: Advanced Arabic language ability.

REL 701.description: Research Seminar in Religious Studies. Skills for academic professionalization, presentation of research in progress and formal responses to academic writing.

RISK 380.description: Introduction to Enterprise Risk Management. Understand the concept of risk, risk assessment, and management frameworks. Learn to identify, analyze, manage and mitigate, and communicate this risk to stakeholders. Duplicates credit in the former ACCT 380.

RISK 385.description: Introduction to Risk Management and Insurance. Understand the underlying economics, structure, and business models of an organization (often an insurance carrier) willing to accept risk for diverse situations: property, life, healthcare. Duplicates credit in the former ACCT 385.

RISK 387.description: Risk Management in Entertainment, Sports and the Arts. Knowledge and skills needed to identify, analyze, control, finance and report on the risks particular to entertainment, sports and the arts. Duplicates credit in the former ACCT 387.

RISK 388.description: Innovating Risk Solutions in Disruptive Environments. Develop the skills needed to think critically about identified and assessed risks and develop innovative solutions to control and transfer those risks. Duplicates credit in the former ACCT 388.

RISK 580.description: Advanced Enterprise Risk Management. The practical application of enterprise risk management across a broad spectrum of business settings and industry types, from start-up to multinational organizations.

RISK 583.description: The Top Five Risks and What to Do About Them. Examination of what boards and management at large and midsize companies think are the top five risks in business.

RISK 599.description: Special Topics. Current developments in the field of Risk Management. Topics vary from semester to semester. May be repeated only if topic is different.

RUSS 120.description: Beginning Russian I. Introduction to the Russian language with emphasis on basic conversational skills, major points of grammar and reading.

RUSS 150.description: Beginning Russian II. Continuation of RUSS 120.

RUSS 220.description: Intermediate Russian I. Development of thematic conversational skills with emphasis on extended dialogue. Review of basic morphology with special attention to verbs of motion. Reading of authentic material is emphasized.

RUSS 310.description: Advanced Russian in Popular Culture. Advanced conversation, reading, grammar and topical analysis of Russian press, films and other popular sources. Conducted in Russian.

RUSS 500.description: Topics in Advanced Russian. Study of Russian required for graduate work and professional activities.

MSCR 490.description: Directed Research.  Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit. Duplicates credit in former MUCH 490. Open only to Juniors and Seniors.

MSCR 590.description: Directed Research. Research leading to the Master's Degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC. Duplicates credit in former MUCH 590.

MSCR 790.description: Research. Research leading to the doctorate. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC. Duplicates credit in former MUCH 790.

SCOR 403.description: Introduction to Scoring Movies and Television. Practical composition course covering the unique art, craft, and technology involved in writing and integrating music for animated and live-action visual media.

SCOR 405.description: Introduction to Scoring Video Games. Practical composition course covering the unique art, craft, and technology involved in composing and integrating video-game music.

SCOR 490.description: Directed Research. Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit.

SCOR 501.description: Individual Instruction. Secondary instruction for graduate music majors or instruction for graduate non-music majors.

SCOR 502.description: Individual Instruction in Advanced Screen Scoring. Individual instruction and review of students work. Selected composers, orchestrators, filmmakers, and other important industry collaborators offer their insights on scoring and career building.

SCOR 503A.description: Advanced Scoring for Motion Pictures and Television. Scoring principles involved in designing, timing, and composing scores for video projects, including documentaries, animated, and live-action projects. Will also include composing for live recording sessions.

SCOR 504A.description: Orchestral Scoring. Explores the sounds of and notations for the major orchestral instruments; provides instruction on implementation of those instruments in scoring and orchestrating for the screen.

SCOR 505A.description: Advanced Game Scoring and Integration. Explores more sophisticated principles and techniques involved in the unique aspects of composing and integrating music for video games.

SCOR 506.description: Applied Techniques in Contemporary Scoring. Explores the most recent artistic and technological innovations in film/television scoring, and includes creating cues from adapted themes.

SCOR 507.description: Studio Conducting and Contemporary Score Analysis. Study of two distinct areas: 1) The methods and protocols involved in conducting scoring sessions; and 2) Analysis of innovative scores from current television- and feature- films.

SCOR 511A.description: History of Film Scoring. Examines the evolution of movie music from 1920s to present. Includes recorded interviews with the most significant film composers and film clips of their work.

SCOR 521A.description: Recording, Mixing and Editing for the Screen Composer. Addresses the need for modern-day screen composers to produce and digitally record, sweeten, mix, and edit much of their own music.

SCOR 523A.description: Advanced Screen Scoring Technology. Explores sophisticated principles and applications of technologies for screen scoring, including the use of synthesizers, samplers, and sequencers.

SCOR 590.description: Directed Research. Research leading to the Master's Degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

SCOR 790.description: Research. Research leading to the doctorate. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department.

SLL 110.description: Russia in the Modern Era. Key moments in the development of Russian culture since its westernization in the early eighteenth century to the present day. Focus on works of literature, art and other products of the culture that have significantly influenced Russian self-understanding as well as the ways in which Russians perceive the rest of the world.

SLL 199.description: Chess and Critical Thinking. Analysis of significant chess games, reflecting societal attitudes  towards science, competition, art, gender, psychology, politics,  and technology.  Graded CR/NC.

SLL 345.description: Literature and Philosophy: Dostoevsky. Dostoevsky's novels as psychological and philosophical analyses of modern alienated man. Readings in Dostoevsky and selections from Gide, Kafka, Camus, and Sartre. Conducted in English.

SLL 501.description: Proseminar in Russian Literature. Introduction to graduate study of Russian literature; research methods, bibliography, transliteration, development of critical writing skills.

SLL 523.description: Methods of Teaching Russian as a Foreign Language. Introduces future Assistant Lecturers to the communicative method of teaching Russian and focuses on theories and methods of teaching the language, as well as key concepts of second language acquisition.

SLL 532.description: 18th Century Russian Literature. Major works and genres of the 18th century. The development of a "modern" literary tradition, focusing on the problems of Russia's indigenization of Western literary movements (classicism and sentimentalism.)

SLL 546.description: The Russian Novel.  Genre of the novel as exemplified in the works of one or more Russian authors. Readings from Gogol, Turgenev, Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, and others. Prerequisite: three years of college Russian.

SLL 590.description: Directed Research.  Research leading to the Master's degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

SLL 660.description: Seminar on Single Author or Work. Theme varies from year to year. An author or major work will be    selected for intensive study; research paper required. May be      repeated, with departmental permission, if content of the seminar  is different. Recommended preparation: one year of graduate study.

SLL 790.description: Research. Research leading to the doctorate. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

SOWK 110.description: Thriving: Connecting Wellness, Identity and  Systems. A dynamic exploration of how humans thrive -- blending science, creativity and culture to inspire resilience and social connection while linking personal well-being to collective transformation.

SOWK 300.description: Foundations of Social Work. Explore foundations of social work in this introductory course:    history, ethics, roles, communication, cultural competence,        advocacy and human rights.

SOWK 350.description: Adolescent Gang Intervention. The incidence of gangs (particularly in the Los Angeles area),  gang interventions, and policies developed to address the growing  gang situation.

SOWK 390.description: Special Problems.  Supervised, individual studies. No more than one registration permitted. Enrollment by petition only.

SOWK 424.description: Community Experience in Juvenile Justice Environments. Provides in-class and on-site community experiences to increase knowledge and understanding of youth experience in a range of social environments focused on juvenile justice.

SOWK 506.description: Human Behavior and the Social Environment. The person-in-environment, bio-psycho-social perspective is the lens through which theories of personality, family, group, organization, community, culture and their interactions are explored. (Duplicates credit in SOWK 503 and SOWK 505)

SOWK 510.description: Professional Self-Care in Integrative Social Work Practice. Focuses on the value, examination and integration of professional self-care, wellness and resilience strategies into ethical and professional integrative social work practice.

SOWK 511.description: Critical Decision Making in Integrative Social Work Practice. Focuses on the value and application of critical thinking and decision-making into ethical and professional integrative social work practice.

SOWK 523.description: Foundations of Integrative Social Work Practice I. Principles underlying social work practice with emphasis on rapport building, engagement, assessment and contracting individuals, families and groups though a social change framework.

SOWK 525.description: Foundations of Integrative Social Work Practice II. Principles underlying social work practice with emphasis on intervention, termination and evaluation with individuals, families and groups though a social change framework.

SOWK 536.description: Policy and Advocacy in Professional Social Work. A study of the complex and interconnecting systems of policy, programs and communities that directly and indirectly impact Social Workers' clients lives. (Duplicates credit in SOWK 534)

SOWK 546.description: Science of Social Work. Introduction to the role of scientific inquiry in advancing social work goals. Inspires students to include science in their social work identity and professional decision-making. (Duplicates credit in SOWK 562)

SOWK 591.description: Applied Learning in Practicum Education I. Practicum seminar and placement for developing foundational skills in integrative social work practice with individuals, families, groups, communities and/or organizations.

SOWK 593.description: Applied Learning in Practicum Education II. Practicum seminar and placement for developing foundational skills in integrative social work practice with individuals, families, groups, communities and/or organizations.

SOWK 604.description: Social Work Perspectives on Contemporary Challenges in Educa. Provides a holistic understanding of the current issues students and their families must confront. Explores interventions grounded in evidence, best practice models, strength-based and asset-driven.

SOWK 608.description: Research and Evaluation in Integrative Social Work Practice. Critical analysis and application of empirical evidence and research methods to assess client strengths and needs and to evaluate and improve integrative social work practice.

SOWK 609.description: Advanced ISW Practice II: Schools and Educational Settings. Critical application of theory, evidence and professional standards for integrative and culturally responsive assessment and intervention, highlighting practice contexts involving schools and educational settings

SOWK 612.description: Assessment and Diagnosis of Mental Disorders. Assessment of mental disorders, and the rationale and organization of the system for diagnosis. Emphasis is on developing differential diagnostic skills.

SOWK 614.description: Advanced ISW Practice I: Schools and Educational Settings. Advanced policy analysis, engagement strategies and human rights advocacy in integrative social work, highlighting practice contexts involving schools and educational settings

SOWK 615.description: Brief Therapy and Crisis Intervention. Theory and multimodal approaches for brief therapy and crisis intervention with a broad spectrum of clients in a range of mental health and health settings.

SOWK 617.description: Substance Related and Behavioral Addictive Disorders and Rec. Causal exploration of substance related and behavioral addictive disorders. Evidence-based and practice informed treatment models for vulnerable individuals, groups and families.

SOWK 619.description: Social Work in Public Child Welfare Settings. Provides tools to enhance the practitioner's repsonse ot the  special challenges (substance abuse, HIV/AIDS, domestic violence)  in public child welfare.

SOWK 627.description: Advanced ISW Practice I: Children, Youth and Families. Advanced policy analysis, engagement strategies and human rights advocacy in integrative social work, highlighting practice contexts involving children, youth and families.

SOWK 630.description: Self-Awareness and Intercultural Humility in  Social Work. Critical exploration of sociocultural context and one's own  values/assumptions/biases to enhance intercultural humility in  social work.

SOWK 642.description: Advanced ISW Practice II: Children, Youth and Families. Critical application of theory, evidence and professional standards for integrative and culturally responsive assessment and intervention, highlighting practice contexts involving children, youth and families.

SOWK 643.description: Advanced ISW Practice I: Adult Mental Health and Wellness. Advanced policy analysis, engagement strategies and human rights advocacy in integrative social work, highlighting practice contexts involving adult mental health and wellness.

SOWK 647.description: Advanced ISW Practice II: Adult Mental Health and Wellness. Critical application of theory, evidence and professional standards for integrative and culturally responsive assessment and intervention, highlighting practice contexts involving adult mental health and wellness.

SOWK 665.description: Grant Writing and Program Development for Social Workers. Grant writing and program development that are generalized to any settings and relevant to direct and macro social work practice expertise.

SOWK 677.description: Mental Health Assessment and Diagnosis of Children and Adole. Mental health assessment and diagnosis of children and adolescents. Course includes relevant diagnoses and the systematic or societal challenges that impact mental health of youth.

SOWK 686.description: Advanced ISW Practice I: Military and Veteran Social Work. Advanced policy analysis, engagement strategies and human rights advocacy in integrative social work, highlighting practice contexts involving military and veteran social work.

SOWK 689.description: Advanced ISW Practice II: Military and Veteran Social Work. Critical application of theory, evidence and professional standards for integrative and culturally responsive assessment, and intervention highlighting practice contexts involving military and veteran social work.

SOWK 691.description: Applied Learning In Practicum Education III. Practicum seminar and placement for developing advanced skills in integrative social work practice with individuals, families, groups, communities and/or organizations.

SOWK 693.description: Applied Learning in Practicum Education IV. Practicum seminar and placement for developing advanced skills in integrative social work practice with individuals, families, groups, communities and/or organizations.

SOWK 703.description: Explanatory and Predictive Theories in Social Work Research. Multi-level theories to guide social work research, emphasizing original texts and theory integration to explain complex social and psychological phenomena.

SOWK 704.description: Complex Social Problems. Emphasizes leadership in addressing systemic social challenges.

SOWK 705.description: Leadership and Strategic Communication for Stakeholder Engag. Leading public discourse for the purposes of increasing civic engagement and public participation, building broad based public support and enabling competencies.

SOWK 706.description: Leadership for Intervention Implementation in Complex System. Examining large scale national, state and local intervention programs as well as modeling potential organizational redesign to improve service delivery strategies.

SOWK 707.description: Financial Management for Social Change. Senior financial management and planning in human service organizations, emphasizing fiscal approaches that focus on strategy, including how to maximize revenue, control costs, allocate resources, improve decision-making and support successful social programs and disruptive social change.

SOWK 711.description: Design Laboratory for Social Innovation I. Incorporates leadership in intervention design, stakeholder engagement, and evidence-based practices.

SOWK 713.description: Research Methods for Intervention Design and Evaluation. Introduction to doctoral-level applied research and evaluation methods, emphasizing the selection, design and application of methods for intervention design and evaluation in complex social contexts.

SOWK 714.description: Executive Leadership: Leaders as Maestros. The Leader/Maestro Concept enlarges the student from a virtuoso perspective - individual performance - to include an organizational performance in leading, creating and measuring change.

SOWK 720.description: Leadership Communication for Social Impact. Mastering communication for social impact. Students will learn the power of listening, consensus-based facilitation, storytelling for social change and communicating with brevity.

SOWK 721.description: Data Driven Decision Making in Social Services. Practical introduction to using quantitative administrative data to identify trends, track performance, evaluate programs and drive decision making.

SOWK 723.description: Design Laboratory for Social Innovation II. Emphasizes leadership in developing responsive interventions to address complex social problems.

SOWK 725A.description: Preparatory Scholarship for Capstone. Design and develop an innovative, feasible, and defensible Capstone Project focusing on a selected Grand Challenge for Social Work.

SOWK 725B.description: Preparatory Scholarship for Capstone. Refine a fully implementable, innovatively designed Grand Challenge Capstone Project. Future-focused on garnering support, piloting and launching students' capstone prototype.

SOWK 725C.description: Preparatory Scholarship for Capstone. Complete a fully implementable, innovatively designed Grand Challenge Capstone Project. Future-focused on garnering support, piloting and launching students' capstone project.

SOWK 760.description: Statistics in Social Work I: Bivariate Analysis and Regressi. Essential building blocks of statistical analysis, including foundation for descriptive and inferential statistics and univariate/bivariate/multivariate analyses.

SOWK 762.description: Social Work Research Methods I. Foundations of social work research, including inquiry models, problem formulation, measurement, design, sampling, data sources, for developing critical understanding of research questions and methodological approaches

SOWK 764.description: Statistics in Social Work II: Categorical Data Analysis. Introduction to single equation statistical modeling using limited dependent variables, including dichotomous, ordered categorical and other outcome forms. Methods are drawn from statistics and econometrics.

SOWK 770.description: Introduction to Qualitative and Mixed Research Methods. Overview of the use of qualitative and mixed methods in social, clinical and health services research.

SOWK 782.description: Doctoral Seminar I: Developing Essential Academic Skills. Introduction to social work graduate student life. Facilitates students socialization into the social work discipline and development of critical academic skills.

SOWK 790.description: Research.  Research leading to the doctorate. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

SOWK 794B.description: Doctoral Dissertation.  Credit on acceptance of dissertation.
