SOCI 150.description: Social Problems. Identifying and analyzing contemporary American social problems, their causes and potential solutions; examines poverty, crime, inequality, education, social isolation and civic decline.

SOCI 155.description: Immigrant America. Examination of the immigrant experience in the United States. Comparative analysis of social context of migration, formation of immigrant communities, and social integration of immigrants.

SOCI 169.description: Changing Family Forms. The peculiarity of the "modern" Western family system in historical and cross-cultural perspective; focus on the "postmodern" family crisis in the United States.

SOCI 200.description: Introduction to Sociology.  Basic concepts of sociology with special reference to group life,social institutions, and social processes.

SOCI 235.description: Migration, Law and Society. Migration policies worldwide are negotiated by different stakeholders and create different contexts of reception that differently impact the everyday lives and livelihoods of migrants.

SOCI 242.description: Sociology, Demography and Health. Sociological and demographic concepts focusing on the causes of disease, health and wellness. Empirical analysis of population composition and its connection to health.

SOCI 250.description: Grassroots Participation in Global Perspective. Theory and history behind the ideal of "the local, grassroots volunteer": a direct link between theory and research using Los Angeles as a case study.

SOCI 255.description: Sociology of Globalization. This course examines globalization through social and economic processes and its consequences for social conflict, economic development, human rights, social movements, and national identity.

SOCI 270.description: Sociological Theory. Historical and contemporary approaches to sociological theory; analysis of conceptual frameworks applied to the study of society and social interaction.

SOCI 313.description: Sociological Research Methods. Logic of theory construction, research design, elementary data collection and analysis.

SOCI 314.description: Analyzing Social Statistics. Sociological measurement, univariate description, elementary correlation, introduction to statistical inference.

SOCI 325.description: Applied Social Research Methods. Use quantitative or qualitative analysis skills to study major social issues using large existing survey data sets or qualitative methods. Become conversant in describing data to a variety of audiences.

SOCI 351.description: Youth, Social Control and Public Policy. Construction of meanings of adolescence, social change and social control. Examines how social institutions such as school, law enforcement, and the state impose social control and how this varies by race, class and gender.

SOCI 360.description: Social Inequality: Class, Status and Power. Inequalities in wealth, prestige and power in the United States; the American class structure and the extent of upward mobility in that structure.

SOCI 369.description: The Family in a Changing Society. Changing family patterns; personality development; family unity, predicting success in marriage; the family in transition; crises such as economic changes, death, divorce; family reorganization.

SOCI 400.description: Field and Survey Experiments. Conducting experiments to estimate causal effects, in the field and using surveys.

SOCI 431.description: Cities. Organization of urban society, including such topics as segregation, urban decay, local politics, residential change and community conflict.

SOCI 450.description: Non-Governmental Organizations/Non-profits Field Practicum. Internship in a Non-Governmental Organization (NGO). Students will conduct sociological research on issues surrounding NGOs and the work they do.

SOCI 464.description: Sociology of Gender and Work. Examination of gender inequality in the U.S. labor market; work-family conflict; employer remedies; comparative social policy.

SOCI 475.description: Medical Sociology.  Social and cultural factors in causation of disease, health care utilization and health care delivery.

SOCI 490.description: Directed Research.  Individual research and readings. Not available for graduate credit.

SOCI 500.description: Sociology Professional Seminar. Introduces students to the theoretical questions and methodological approaches that comprise the discipline of sociology. Experts in each subfield share their latest research with students.

SOCI 510.description: Sociological Theory I. Developments in sociological theory from the discipline's nineteenth century origins to World War II.

SOCI 521.description: Quantitative Methods and Statistics I. Introduction to the logic and tools of quantitative analysis in sociology; covers the basic elements of designing research, summarizing and exploring patterns in data, and making generalizations about populations based on characteristics of samples.

SOCI 590.description: Directed Research.  Research leading to the master's degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

SOCI 593.description: Practicum in Teaching the Liberal Arts. Practical principles for the long-term development of effective teaching within college disciplines. Intended for teaching assistants in Dornsife College. Graded CR/NC.

SOCI 620.description: Advanced Methods--Qualitative Research. Seminar and practicum in conducting and interpreting original qualitative research. Prerequisite: SOCI 520. Duplicates credit in former SOCI 524.

SOCI 655.description: Seminar in Race Relations. Current racial problems in the United States and other countries; critiques of literature on race relations. Duplicates credit in former SOCI 555.

SOCI 790.description: Research.  Research leading to the doctorate. Maximum units which may be     applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded   CR/NC.

SPAN 120.description: Spanish I.  For students with limited proficiency in Spanish. Practice in     listening comprehension, oral communication, elementary reading    and writing.

SPAN 150.description: Spanish II. Continuation of Spanish 110 or 120; increased emphasis on listening comprehension, oral expression, reading and writing.

SPAN 220.description: Spanish III. Continuation of SPAN 150; intensive work in listening comprehension, oral communication, reading, and writing with emphasis on free expression; readings related to Hispanic culture and civilization. Prereq: SPAN 150 or equivalent.

SPAN 240.description: Spanish IV. Intensive review of Spanish grammar with emphasis on four skills. Audio-visual materials and readings related to Hispanic culture and civilization.

SPAN 260.description: Advanced Spanish: Arts and Sciences.  Development of students' oral and writing skills using literary and scientific materials; grammar review. Duplicates credit in the former SPAN 266.

SPAN 280.description: Conversational Spanish. Discussions of short films, cultural and literary texts and other activities designed to improve conversational skills. Prerequisite: SPAN 220. Not for credit for Spanish majors.

SPAN 290.description: Introduction to Latin American and Iberian       Studies                                         . Introduction to the cultural history of Spain, Portugal and Latin America with a focus on literature and visual works from the early-modern period to the twenty-first century.

SPAN 301.description: Introduction to Literature and Film. Introduction to critical reading and interpretation of poetry, narrative fiction, drama and film from Spain and Latin America.

SPAN 302.description: Screen Cultures: From Film to the Internet. A survey of Spanish and Latin American cinema from the silent film era to the present, acquainting students with various critical and theoretical approaches to cinema studies. Conducted in Spanish.

SPAN 308.description: The Art of Poetry. A survey of Spanish and Latin American poetry from the Middle Ages to the present, acquainting students with various critical and theoretical approaches to verse. Conducted in Spanish.

SPAN 310.description: Structure of Spanish. A systematic study of the structure of Spanish. Topics include fundamental aspects of the sound system; word classes; sentences and their meaning; linguistic change and variation; standard and colloquial usage.

SPAN 316.description: Spanish for the Professions. The language and culture of a particular area of study or profession, such as medicine and healthcare, political and social sciences, business and the law. Limited to 4 units for major or minor credit.

SPAN 484.description: Studies in Visual and Material Culture. An examination of the role of visual and material culture in cultural and social context in the Hispanic world, focusing on a selected time period and geographical region.

SPAN 545.description: 20th and 21st Century Latin American Literature and Culture. Study of cultural currents, authors, literary texts, films and other media in Latin America in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries.

SPAN 592.description: Practicum in Teaching Spanish . Approaches and techniques in the teaching of Spanish and/or Portuguese as a second language.Open only to Master and Doctoral students in Comparative Literature, Comparative Culture in Literature and Studies (Spanish and Latin American Studies), Linguistics (Hispanic Linguistics) and Spanish.

SSCI 135.description: Maps in the Digital World. The role of formal reasoning, abstract representation and empirical analysis in building maps for sharing knowledge across the physical, life and social sciences and humanities.

SSCI 165.description: Sustainability Science in the City. The influence of sustainability science on public policy and vice versa in the context of social/ethical theories, analytical methods and solutions.

SSCI 175.description: Food, Health and Place. The role of food systems in human nutrition and environmental health, and system transformations needed to achieve good health, equity and sustainability.

SSCI 201.description: Principles of Geodesign. Foundations of geodesign combining place-making, design, collective action, and the science of location-based information to improve human interaction with the functioning of the Earth.

SSCI 202.description: Principles of Geospatial Intelligence. Introduction to basic geospatial intelligence knowledge and related practical applications that assist in informing decision-making in a variety of human security settings.

SSCI 214.description: Human Populations and Natural Hazards. Introduction to the complex relationship between human development and natural hazards, which are increasingly causing damage and displacement to human populations throughout the world.

SSCI 220.description: Spatial Data Collection Using Drones. Develop the requisite knowledge and practical skills to source, analyze, and produce GIS and simulation-based projects with unmanned aerial systems-derived data.

SSCI 265.description: The Water Planet. An exploration of earth's water, ranging from water properties, chemistry, and pollution, to groundwater dynamics, watershed processes, and oceanic-atmospheric circulation. Implications for past and future societies. Lecture and laboratory.

SSCI 301.description: Maps and Spatial Reasoning. Role of maps and spatial reasoning in the production and use of geographic information for representing and analyzing human and environmental activities and events.

SSCI 381.description: Statistics for the Spatial Sciences. Conceptual foundations and techniques of statistics and how they can be used with geographic data to produce actionable information across spatial science domains.

SSCI 397.description: Spatial Sciences Internship. Intensive experience in local public agency, private firm, or nonprofit agency engaged in applied geospatial analysis, modeling and mapping work.

SSCI 490.description: Directed Research.  Individual research and readings. Open only to juniors and seniors. Not available for graduate credit.

SSCI 572.description: GIS and Landscape Architecture. The use of GIS, spatial analysis, modeling, and 2- and 3-D mapping to support landscape architecture projects that span multiple spatiotemporal scales.

SSCI 573.description: Principles and Practices of Geodesign. Principles, frameworks, workflows and case studies of how geography, spatial sciences, place-making and design support collective action to improve human well-being.

SSCI 574.description: Spatial Econometrics. Introduction to the theoretical foundations, methods, and software systems for spatial econometrics using a variety of use cases.

SSCI 575.description: Spatial Data Science. Introduce the spatial data scientific approach to issues and present a holistic generalizable analysis pipeline.

SSCI 577.description: Human Security and Disaster Management. The relationship between human security (population growth, urbanization, conflict) and disasters, both man-made and natural, where complex emergencies are impactful to human populations.

SSCI 581.description: Concepts for Spatial Thinking. The unique characteristics and importance of spatial information as they relate to the evolving science, technology, and applications of Geographic Information Systems.

SSCI 582.description: Spatial Databases. Design, implementation, and interrogation of relational, object-oriented and other types of geospatial databases. Recommended preparation: SSCI 581.

SSCI 583.description: Spatial Analysis and Modeling. Provides the knowledge and skills necessary to investigate the spatial patterns which result from social and physical processes operating at or near the Earth's surface.

SSCI 586.description: GIS Programming and Customization. Design, coding, and implementation of GIS-based software and models using the Python programming language. Recommended preparation: SSCI 582. Duplicates credit in former GEOG 586.

SSCI 587.description: Spatial Data Acquisition. Role of global positioning systems, maps, geocoding, and other kinds of sensors as geospatial data sources. Includes field data acquisition excursion on Catalina Island. Recommended preparation: SSCI-581. Duplicates credit in former GEOG 587.

SSCI 588.description: Remote Sensing for GIS. Principles of remote sensing, satellite systems, and role of remote sensing data in GIS applications. Recommended preparation: SSCI 581.

SSCI 589.description: Cartography and Visualization. Principles of visual perception, spatial cognition and cartographic design and their contributions to the maps, animations, virtual reality and multimedia displays produced with modern GIS. Recommended preparation: SSCI 581.

SSCI 590.description: Directed Research.  Research leading to the master's degree in cognate fields. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Graded CR/NC.

SSCI 591.description: Web and Mobile GIS. Design and implementation of locally served and cloud-based geospatial web applications. Construction of web maps, mashups and Volunteered Geographic Information interfaces.

SSCI 594B.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of thesis. Graded CR/NC.

SSCI 594Z.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of thesis. Graded CR/NC.

SSCI 596.description: Internship in Spatial Sciences. Part-time or full-time practical work experience in the student's field of study at an off-campus facility under faculty direction.

SSCI 600.description: The Geography of Life and Death. Meaning and significance of place and role of social, natural, and built environments in disease occurrence in different places and populations. Open only to doctoral students.

SSCI 681.description: Advanced Quantitative Methods for Population, Health and Pla. Fundamentals of temporal and spatiotemporal data analysis; modern methods for evaluating, managing, and visualizing spatiotemporal data; hands-on use cases.

SSCI 693.description: Practicum in Teaching the Liberal Arts. Principles of pedagogy for teaching the liberal arts, focusing on issues and technologies for spatial thinking. Required for first-semester teaching assistants in spatial sciences.

SSCI 790.description: Research. Research leading to the doctoral degree. Maximum units which may  be applied to the degree to be determined by the department. Open  only to doctoral students.

SCRM 310.description: Laboratory Techniques in Developmental and Stem Cell Biology. Laboratory course that focuses on the theory and practice of embryology to study developmental biology, and cell culture to study stem cell biology.

SCRM 490.description: Directed Research. Individual research and readings under the guidance of a faculty member.

SCRM 510.description: Current Topics in Regenerative Medicine. Selected topics on sub-fields within developmental and stem cell biology including review of contemporary literature and research.

SCRM 511.description: Developmental Biology and Human Embryology. Survey of anatomical, cellular and molecular processes that underlie human development and congenital malformations, with discussion of other species for comparison. Open only to Stem Cell Biology and Regenerative Medicine majors.

SCRM 513.description: Stem Cells and Regenerative Medicine. A comprehensive investigation of embryonic, fetal and adult stem cells and the application of stem cell biology to treat disease. Open only to Stem Cell Biology and Regenerative Medicine majors.

SCRM 525.description: Tools and Techniques in Stem Cell Biology. Introduces students to classical and cutting-edge techniques used to assess stem cells and regenerating systems.

SCRM 555.description: Writing About Stem Cell Biology and Regenerative Medicine. Instruction in writing for various audiences on topics related to stem cell biology and regenerative medicine.

SCRM 580.description: SCRM External Speaker Seminar Series. Reading and discussion of recent papers by the SCRM speaker of the week, and attendance at the speaker's seminar. Open only to Stem Cell Biology and Regenerative Medicine majors.

SCRM 590.description: Independent Research. Independent research conducted under the guidance of faculty in the Department of Stem Cell Biology and Regenerative Medicine.

SCRM 594A.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of Thesis. Graded IP/CR/NC.

SCRM 594B.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of Thesis. Graded IP/CR/NC.

SCRM 594Z.description: Master's Thesis. Credit on acceptance of Thesis. Graded IP/CR/NC.

SCRM 596.description: Internship for Curricular Practical Training. Part- or full-time, practical work experience or research in the  field of stem cell biology and regenerative medicine. Students are  individually supervised by faculty.

SMGT 500.description: Introduction to Sustainability. History and evolution of sustainability, including definitions, models and policies relevant to current global sustainability and advocacy.

SMGT 505.description: Sustainability Fundamentals. Evolution of business sustainability; environmental, social and governance (ESG) performance; and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

SMGT 510.description: Business Strategy for a Sustainable World. Business strategies, practices, and performance metrics that champion sustainability as part of organizational purpose.

SMGT 515.description: Leading Organizational Transformation for Sustainability. Organizational transformation through integration of sustainability into values, culture, leadership, talent, workflow and strategy.

SMGT 520.description: Sustainable Supply and Global Value Chains. Sustainable management of supply chains and global value chains to increase benefits to business, the environment and society.

SMGT 525.description: The Circular Economy and Sustainable Design. Interrelationship of circular economy and sustainable design strategies to reduce waste and negative social and environmental impacts.

SMGT 540.description: Sustainability Strategies for Human Rights. Strategies for businesses to address a range of human rights concerns and monitor their effects on individuals, society and the environment.

SMGT 545.description: Systems Thinking and Tools for Sustainability. Application of systems theory, thinking and tools to address complex sustainability-related problems.

SMGT 550.description: Sustainability Metrics and Reporting. Strategies for organizations to identify, measure and report on prioritized sustainability issues.

SMGT 555.description: Sustainability Management Strategy Capstone. Knowledge and skills gained throughout the Sustainability Management program are synthesized in a culminating capstone project.

SAE 541.description: Systems Engineering Theory and Practice. Integration of engineering problem solving methodologies based on systems concepts. Application to complex, large scale technical systems and problems faced by engineering managers. Case studies.

SAE 547.description: Model-Based Systems Architecting and Engineering. Approaches for modeling systems using software such as SySML; modeling system, requirements, structure, behavior, and parametrics; mapping to hardware description language and behavioral code generation. Recommended preparation: Modeling and simulation courses.

SAE 550.description: Systems Architecting and the Political Process                                                   . Analysis of risks inherent in managing high-tech/high-cost  government-funded engineering programs; tools and techniques for  coping with the impacts of politically-driven budgets on the      engineering design process.  Recommended preparation: 2 years of  work experience.

SAE 560.description: Economic Considerations for Systems Engineering. Impact of economic factors for systems architects and engineers,  tools for understanding these factors, fundamental quantitative  analysis of cash flow, life-cost estimating for systems and  software engineering.

SAE 580.description: Artificial Intelligence for Systems Engineers. Linear modeling, knowledge representation, supervised and unsupervised learning, optimization and evolutionary algorithms; augmented intelligence for decision-making, intelligent monitoring and control; real-world applications.

SAE 590.description: Directed Research. Research leading to the master's degree.  Maximum units which may  be applied to the degree to be determined by the department.   Graded CR/NC.

TAC 100.description: Enhanced Productivity with AI. Enhance  how you think, work, and create by mastering AI tools that amplify focus, creativity, and personal productivity.

TAC 101.description: Business Tools and Digital Fluency. An introduction to the software and technologies used in modern business environments and practices required to effectively function in online environments.

TAC 104.description: Web Development. Core HTML and CSS for building functional, custom websites. Includes responsive design, modern frameworks and AI-assisted tools.

TAC 115.description: Programming in Python. Introduction to Python; intended for students without prior programming experience.

TAC 116.description: Accelerated Programming in Python. Accelerated introduction to Python; intended for students with prior programming experience.

TAC 125.description: Hackers to CEOs: Intro to Cyber Security in the AI Era. Cyber security, threats, intrusions, controls and countermeasures. Hacking computers and humans. Cyber and AI risk. Phishing, social engineering and other human hacking techniques.

TAC 165.description: Introduction to C++ Programming. Introduction to programming using C++, including variables, operators, conditionals, loops, arrays, vectors, strings, functions, files, structs, pointers, dynamic allocation and an introduction to classes.

TAC 168.description: Introduction to MATLAB. Fundamentals of MATLAB: a high-performance numeric computation and visualization environment. Overview of linear algebra and matrix manipulation; using 2-D and 3-D plotting routines; programming in MATLAB; basic numerical analysis.

TAC 180.description: Video Game Production. The process of video game production. Video game history, genres, development process (concept, preproduction, production and post-production) and roles (producers, artists, programmers, etc.).

TAC 190.description: Digital Graphics and UI Design Tools. Learn tools for digital graphics and visual communication using Photoshop, with fundamentals supporting social media, print, presentations and UI design.

TAC 215.description: Introduction to 3D Modeling, Animation and Visual Effects. An applied introduction to the techniques used for modeling, animating, texturing, lighting, rendering, and creating 3D content for games, cinematics, visual effects, animation and visualizations.

TAC 216.description: Applied Python. Development of practical Python programming skills through project-based applications; "Pythonic" ways of solving problems in modern computational domains.

TAC 228.description: Computer-Aided Modeling and Rapid Fabrication. Computer-aided modeling techniques for rapid fabrication. Conceptualize, design, fabricate, assemble and test 3D printed prototypes.

TAC 249.description: Introduction to Data Analytics. Introduction to data analytics. Basics of databases, applied statistics, data visualization. Leverage data to make critical business decisions.

TAC 259.description: Basics of Artificial Intelligence. Concepts and techniques in artificial intelligence; approaches in artificial narrow intelligence; applications of AI that are already changing society; ethical and social questions in AI.

TAC 265.description: Software Design with Object-Oriented Programming. Learn to design and build software systems using object-oriented programming, with a focus on modular thinking, problem solving and real-world applications across disciplines.

TAC 299.description: Special Topics. Selected topics in Technology and Applied Computing.

TAC 303.description: Full-Stack Web Development. Modern web development techniques for building web applications from the ground up. Front-end and back-end development, including databases, JavaScript libraries and web application frameworks.

TAC 304.description: Back-End Web Development. Database design, server-side programming, API development, modern frameworks and the use of AI-assisted tools in back-end development.

TAC 325.description: Ethical Hacking. Ethical hacking; penetration testing; vulnerability assessment; red teams; hacker environments, infrastructure and frameworks; lateral movement and data exfiltration techniques; evasion and anti-forensics.

TAC 348.description: Making Smart Devices: Introduction to Electronics/Wearables. Design of electronic devices that interact with the physical world; electronic interfaces; development of software algorithms; micro-controller implementation.

TAC 351.description: 3D Character Modeling for Games. Character design principles, visual communication and planning for games; polygonal construction, use of image guides and edge flows for realistic deformation.

TAC 357.description: Enterprise Networks: Design and Architecture. Network technologies. Routers and managed switches. Integrated operating systems (IOS). Strategies for endpoint management. Subnets and securing subnetworks. Reliability with networks and network infrastructure.

TAC 359.description: Applied Neural Networks. Design, build, and train applied neural networks to solve real-world problems; implement neural networks for machine vision, image recognition and object detection and tracking.

TAC 370.description: Cybersecurity Management and Operations. Cybersecurity project design. Incident response. Teambuilding, management and communications for cybersecurity. Scalable approaches for implementation of Information Security Management Systems.

TAC 375.description: Digital Forensics and Cybersecurity Investigations. Forensic science techniques. Digital evidence preservation. Processes and methodologies for digital examinations. Cyber crime investigations. Windows file system analysis. Real case scenario analysis and reporting

TAC 376.description: Engineering AI Products. Full-stack engineering of Al-native products from system architecture to deployment and employing the modern technical stack to transform concepts into market-ready software.

TAC 438.description: Advanced Gameplay Programming. Advanced gameplay programming techniques for both single player and networked multiplayer games using an industry-standard game engine.

TAC 445.description: Apple Forensics and Security (macOS and iOS). Digital forensics, evidence collection and analysis of Apple devices including macOS and iOS. Mac, iPhone, iPad and other Apple device analysis.

TAC 450.description: High Performance Computing in Applied Machine Learning. Theoretical and practical high performance computing approaches to various computational methods in applied machine learning.

lectures.instructor: BD Kim; Iman Rahbari; Hao Ji

TAC 458.description: Defending and Investigating Compromised Networks. Designing, building, securing and hardening enterprise network infrastructures, investigating compromised infrastructures; red, purple and blue team capabilities; detecting, following and ejecting attackers.

TAC 459.description: Applied Natural Language Processing and Generative AI. Generative AI and NLP fundamentals through hands-on work with GPT/BERT, covering prompt engineering, RAG, fine-tuning, retrieval, sentiment analysis, QA and machine translation for product building.

TAC 470.description: Technology and Applied Computing Practicum. Independent technology project related to specific topics under    the direction of a faculty member.

TAC 479.description: Cyber Law and Privacy. Cyber legal issues, search and seizure, 4th amendment and digital evidence, warrants, private searches, wiretaps, tracking devices, workplace privacy.

TAC 480.description: Technology and Applied Computing Internship. Practical experience in applying information technology skills in  real-world settings. Supervised internship at companies and        start-ups. Balancing academic rigor with corporate challenges and  deadlines.

TAC 499.description: Special Topics. Recent developments in computers and data processing.

GRSC 800A.description: Studies for the Qualifying Examination. Studies for the Qualifying Examination. Students may enroll in GRSC 800, once they have completed all other degree requirements, to prepare for their Qualifying Examination.

GRSC 803.description: Enrollment for PhD Students on an Approved Health Leave                      . This course is administratively created to ensure continuing PhD  students have access to health insurance and other support while  on an approved health leave.

GRSC 804.description: Enrollment for PhD students on an Approved       Parental Leave                                  . This course is administratively created to ensure continuing PhD  students have access to health insurance and other support while  on an approved parental leave.

GRSC 810.description: Studies for Master's Examination. Completion of all course work for the master's degree and  permission of the Graduate School.  Graded CR/NC.

CORE 101.description: Symbols and Conceptual Systems: Thematic Option Honors Progr. Study of the structures through which we shape our experience in religion, philosophy, literature, music, and the visual arts, and of competing theories of interpretation. Students may not take this course on a P/NP basis.

CORE 102.description: Culture and Values: Thematic Option Honors Program. Systematic reasoning about values and ways of living; close reading of great literary and philosophical works from a range of classical traditions to the present.

CORE 103.description: The Process of Change in Science: Thematic Option Honors Pro. Critical problems in the development of scientific thought, studied as vehicles for understanding the content and structure of the sciences. Specific subject matter in selected scientific disciplines will be presented. Students may not take this course on a P/NP basis.

CORE 104.description: Change and the Future: Thematic Option Honors Program. Analysis of historical change; social and political theory and revolutionary thought; introduction to competing images of future states of affairs; the continuing process of change. Students may not take this course on a P/NP basis.

CORE 111.description: Writing Seminar I: Thematic Option Honors Program. The first level writing course focuses on the relationship between critical thinking and analytic writing through the close reading of primary texts. Seminars are supplemented with biweekly one-on-one tutorials.

CORE 200.description: Liberal Arts Reading Salon. Critical readings of a series of texts in the liberal arts  designed to promote discussion of important themes, theoretical  approaches, research directions, and interdisciplinary  connections.  Graded CR/NC.

CORE 601.description: Teaching Analytical Writing through Readings in the Humanities. Theories and practices in university-level teaching of  close-reading and analytical writing, using texts central to  Western tradition.  Graduate student professionalization throught  topical workshops and discussions.  Open to assistant lecturers  and teaching assistants only.  Graded CR/NC.

TRGN 510.description: Basic Foundations in Translational Biomedical Informatics. Translational biomedical informatics analysis of next-generation sequencing genomic data, fundamentals, foundations, and concepts for applied analysis, human ontology, application molecular tools, basic computing.

TRGN 514.description: Introduction to Human Genomic Analysis Methods. Translational next generation sequencing genomics microarrays, RNA-seq, exome sequencing, annotation, transcriptome, ontology, pipelines, variants, expression, methylation.

TRGN 520.description: Translational Biomedical Informatics Capstone Portfolio. Portfolio, translational biomedical informatics, bioinformatics, genomics, application development, web-based application.

TRGN 539.description: Translational Biotechnology Practicum. Experiential training based on a project in a biomedical, biotechnology or pharmaceutical setting.

TRGN 540.description: Translational Biotechnology Capstone Preparation. Preparation for capstone defense course.

TRGN 541.description: Translational Biotechnology Capstone Defense. Finalization and defense of capstone project.

TRGN 543.description: Biotechnology Entrepreneurship and Commercialization I. Global biotechnology industry, idea generation, business plan formulation, intellectual property protection, funding, personnel management including board composition, regulatory body interaction, company exits.

TRGN 545.description: Exploring Chemical and Biological Therapeutic Modalities. Turning molecules into drugs and cells into therapeutics. Emphasizing selection, development and optimization of appropriate modalities to target specific key defects in diseases.

TRGN 550.description: Communicating Science: Writing. Written communication modalities for accurate and effective transmission of scientific information to a wide audience in biomedical, healthcare, and related industries.

TRGN 590.description: Directed Research. Research leading to the master's degree. Maximum units which may be applied to the degree to be determined by the department.

TRGN 599.description: Special Topics. Selected topics in Translational Genomics.

UGST 001.description: First Year Transition and Success. Addresses first-year academic exploration at USC and covers student success practices. Includes instructor lectures and faculty/staff presentations on academic exploration, strengths development, mindset, resilience, grit, study strategies, time management, campus resources, careers and high-impact practices.

USC 099.description: WBB Semester At Large. This is a zero unit, zero cost class to maintain USC student  status for WBB students while they are away studying at KHUST and  Bocconi.  Enrollment in this class will grant full time student  status at USC with access to student services.

USC 100.description: TEMPORARY ENROLLMENT/FILL COURSE. The registration for this course should only be temporary. There is no instruction in this course. (Used for special purposes by Registration.)

USC 300.description: Overseas Block Enrollment. Block enrollment course for registration purposes only.

USC 300O.description: Off-Campus Studies. Course created to accomodate situations in which students enrolled  in block overseas enrollment courses fail to complete the course.   Depending upon the particular circumstances, the student will be  assigned a mark of W or NC.

USC 500O.description: Off Campus Studies            . Off campus coursework; course serves as a block enrollment until  transcript from host institution is provided and can be  articulated into an MOI that results in individual courses on the  USC transcript with section titles that reflect the title of the  course at the host institution.

PLUS 650.description: Public Policy and Globalization. Challenges of public policymaking and administration; conceptual foundations of public policy as well as the practical and political constraints on government action; theories, models, and analytical frameworks both domestic and abroad.

PLUS 694A.description: Planning, Design and Development Professional Dissertation . Credit on acceptance of Planning, Design and Development Professional Dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC.

PLUS 694B.description: Planning, Design and Development Professional Dissertation. Credit on acceptance of Planning, Design and Development Professional Dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC.

PLUS 694C.description: Planning, Design and Development Professional Dissertation. Credit on acceptance of Planning, Design and Development Professional Dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC.

PLUS 694D.description: Planning, Design and Development Professional Dissertation . Credit on acceptance of Planning, Design and Development Professional Dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC.

PLUS 694Z.description: Planning, Design and Development Professional   Dissertation                                    . Credit on acceptance of Planning, Design and Development Professional Dissertation. Graded IP/CR/NC.

VISS 501.description: Introduction to Visual Studies:  Methods and Debates. A critical introduction to the field of visual studies focusing on interdisciplinary approaches to images, objects, and visual technologies as well as key texts and interpretive debates.

CTWR 100.description: Story: Character, Conflict, and Catharsis. Fundamentals course on the elements of scene writing, story structure, and character development.

CTWR 120.description: Genesis of the Screenplay . The evolution of the screenplay from its roots in myths, plays, and short stories. Writing original treatments for film and television inspired by literary masters.

CTWR 206A.description: Writing the Screenplay. Development of synopsis and treatment for a theatrical or documentary screenplay: theme, plot, character, mise-en-scene and utilization of cinematic elements.

CTWR 303.description: From Page to Screen: Adapting Stories for Film and TV. Detailed investigation of source material and how it translates to screen. Special attention paid to character, genre and story as relates to intellectual property.

CTWR 305.description: Advanced Screenwriting: The Relationship Screenplay. An inquiry into the complex nature of human relationships by writing an original feature length screenplay that examines the multidimensional world of characters and the ties that bind them together.

CTWR 316.description: Advanced Script Analysis. Advanced critical analysis of story and character across film, television, and other mediums. Identification of key story elements of structure, character and emotion journey.

CTWR 321.description: Breaking the Hour-Long Television Series. Introduction to hour-long television staff writing. Breaking of a complete season and writing episodes. Special attention to season construction, pitching, character and story engine.

CTWR 324.description: Breaking the Half-Hour Television Series. The fundamentals of writing for half-hour television. Writing an episode of an existing half-hour television series, with emphasis on conception, pitching, characterization and structure.

CTWR 400.description: Is This A Joke: Mechanics of Comedy Writing. Intensive fundamental writing class for all forms of comedy writing including joke construction, late night, sketches, scene work, and stand-up.

CTWR 404.description: Foundations of Comedy . Study of comedy theory and practical applications in film, television, and social media. Lectures and screenings of comedic forms tracing past, present and future.

CTWR 409.description: Fundamentals of Screenwriting: Character, Conflict and Story. Introduction to writing compelling scenes, creating authentic characters, three-act structure and feature film outlining.

CTWR 413.description: Writing the Short Script I. Preparation of scripts for short films: form, structure, planning. Open only to Cinematic Arts Film and Television Production majors.

CTWR 414.description: The Screenplay. Students study story structure and develop several story outlines, write a short script for possible production, a feature film outline and first act. Recommended preparation: CTWR-416. Open only to Cinematic Arts Film and Television Production majors.

CTWR 416.description: Motion Picture Script Analysis. Critical analysis of story structure from classic films to  contemporary works. Identification of key story concepts and  elements of three-act structure. 2.0, not repeatable.

CTWR 417.description: Script Coverage and Story Analysis. Evaluation of completed scripts prior to their production.  Coverage and analysis of scripts as potential properties from the  perspective of a production company.

CTWR 418A.description: Senior Thesis. a: Creation of feature-length treatment and first draft Senior Thesis screenplay, including "pitching" experiences. B: Completion and revision of Senior Thesis project and introduction to motion picture industry procedures and practices through interaction with industry representatives.  Open to B.F.A. Writing for Screen and  Television students only.

CTWR 419A.description: Senior Thesis in Dramatic Television. Advanced workshop developing an original hour-long dramatic series including characters, world, and story lines for season one. Final assignment is completed hour-long pilot episode.

CTWR 422.description: Creating the Dramatic Television Series . Examination and creation of the world, characters, and concept for an original hour-long dramatic series. Writing an outline for an original dramatic pilot.

CTWR 423.description: Writing the Screenplay. Introduction to formal elements of the screenplay through lectures and the workshopping of a complete first draft of a feature-length script.

CTWR 431.description: Screenwriters and Their Work. Detailed investigation of a specific screenwriter's style and the works they've influenced. Lectures include screenings and visiting screenwriters.

CTWR 435.description: Writing for Film and Television Genres. Preparation of proposals and scripts for different types of film or television programming: emphasis on conception, structure, characterization and format.

CTWR 437.description: Writing the Original Situation Comedy Pilot. Advanced workshop for writing an original half-hour comedy series, including a pilot script, summary of characters and story lines for first season.

CTWR 439.description: Writing the Original Dramatic Series Pilot. Advanced workshop in creation of an original dramatic series, including a first draft of the pilot and a summary of characters and storylines.

CTWR 455.description: Pitching for Film, Television and New Media. Emphasis of verbal storytelling and presentation skills in motion pictures, television, and new media with concentration on story and character.

CTWR 489A.description: Straight to Series:  Writing and Producing the   Episodic Drama                                  . Staff writing and producing the original episodic drama, from development to post-production.

CTWR 505.description: Creating the Short Film. Strengthening and deepening the ability to conceive and develop  ideas that will lead to compelling, authentic, and personally  meaningful films.  Duplicates credit in CTWR 528.

CTWR 512.description: Screenwriting: Imagination and Technique. Intensive introductory course in writing for the screen with emphasis on developing imagination and specific screenwriting techniques, culminating in an original short screenplay.

CTWR 515A.description: Practicum in Screenwriting. Creation of a feature screenplay from presentation through treatment, including some scene work.

CTWR 516.description: Advanced Motion Picture Script Analysis. Critical analysis of the structure of films from the classics to  current award winners.  Students will learn how to identify key  story concepts and break down three act structure in finished  films and scripts.

CTWR 517A.description: Thesis in Half-Hour Television Comedy. Developing an original half-hour comedy television series, including characters, world and storylines for season one. Completion of a first draft script, polish, and series bible.

CTWR 519A.description: Thesis in Television Drama. Part A -- writing the pilot -- is an intensive workshop in which master's students develop an original television 1-hour series including characters, world and storylines for season one. Final assignment is the finished pilot episode of the series.

CTWR 520.description: Advanced Scene Writing Workshop. Intensive workshop oriented specifically to writing and rewriting the most effective and telling dramatic scenes to heighten audience participation and greater story impact.

CTWR 521.description: Advanced Hour-Long Television Drama. Writing the first draft and revision of an episode of an existing dramatic television series.

CTWR 523.description: Introduction to the Screenplay. Introduction to formal elements of the screenplay through lectures and the workshopping of a complete first draft of a feature-length script. Prerequisite: CTAN 536 or CTWR 505 or CTWR 518. Recommended preparation: CTWR 516.

CTWR 529.description: Intermediate Screenwriting. Emphasizes structural elements crucial to the feature film. Techniques for creating an original or adapted theatrical-length script.

CTWR 533.description: Rewriting the Feature Screenplay. Rewriting the feature-length screenplay.  Focus on macro to micro approach to revision.

CTWR 534.description: Advanced Half-Hour Television Comedy. Advanced workshop in writing the first draft and revision of an episode of an existing comedic television series. The comedy writing room will be emphasized.

CTWR 543.description: The Character-Driven Screenplay. Advanced screenwriting wherein a first draft of a feature-length script will be developed and written with an emphasis on character as story engine.

CTWR 553.description: Advanced Rewriting Workshop. Advanced feature screenwriting, emphasizing the rewrite of a first draft script.

CTWR 559.description: The Business of Writing for Screen and Television . Examination and in-depth analysis of the studio system, the television development process, literary representation, new emerging markets, and the Writers Guild of America.

CTWR 572.description: Practicum in Directing Actors for Film.  Seminar in directing actors for film; emphasis on demonstration and laboratory exercises, script analysis, and study and character motivations.

CTWR 585.description: Advanced Genre Writing. Development and execution of writing in various genres of film, television, or new media scripts. Prerequisite: CTWR 514b.

WRIT 150.description: Writing and Critical Reasoning--Thematic Approaches. Academic writing, emphasizing analysis and argumentation, rhetorical judgment, critical reasoning, creative insight, the careful use of evidence, ethical perspectives, logical organization, stylistic and grammatical fluency. Duplicates credit in WRIT 130 and WRIT 140.

WRIT 320.description: Experiential Learning. A writing workshop that allows students to deepen their writing skills while working collaboratively with diverse groups, programs, or populations outside of USC.

WRIT 340.description: Advanced Writing and Critical Engagement. Advanced writing emphasizing critical engagement with disciplinary  practices and ethics, enabling students to produce effective  professional writing and participate responsibly in public  discourse.

WRIT 440.description: Writing in Practical Contexts. Advanced training in analytical and argumentative writing for particular purposes in professional and practical contexts.

WRIT 501A.description: Theory and Practice in Teaching Expository Writing. Pedagogical application of rhetorical and linguistic theory to teaching university-level expository writing. Accompanies supervised teaching. Limited to assistant lecturers and teaching assistants. Graded CR/NC.
